declarations.docstring:
Let $\frac a b\in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ with $b$ squarefree. Are there integers $1 < n_1 < \dots < n_k$,
each the product of two distinct primes, such that $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/306](https://www.erdosproblems.com/306)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (q : ℚ),
    0 < q →
      Squarefree q.den →
        ∃ k n,
          n 0 = 1 ∧
            StrictMono n ∧
              (∀ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k),
                  ArithmeticFunction.cardDistinctFactors (n i) = 2 ∧ ArithmeticFunction.cardFactors (n i) = 2) ∧
                q = ∑ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k), 1 / ↑(n i)

declarations.docstring:
Every positive integer can be expressed as an Egyptian fraction where each denominator is the
product of three distinct primes.
references: [erdosproblems.com/306](https://www.erdosproblems.com/306)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (m : ℕ),
  0 < m →
    ∃ k > 0,
      ∃ n,
        n 0 = 1 ∧
          ∀ (i : ℕ) (hik : i < k),
            n ⟨i, ⋯⟩ < n ⟨i + 1, ⋯⟩ ∧
              (∀ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k),
                  ArithmeticFunction.cardDistinctFactors (n i) = 3 ∧ ArithmeticFunction.cardFactors (n i) = 3) ∧
                ↑m = ∑ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k), 1 / ↑(n i)

declarations.docstring:
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$
1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right)
$$
?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., _Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program._
references: [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ P Q, (∀ p ∈ P, Nat.Prime p) ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, Nat.Prime q) ∧ 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (↑p)⁻¹) * ∑ q ∈ Q, (↑q)⁻¹

declarations.docstring:
A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at
least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by
symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full
`sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean` at tag `v1.0.0`): the left conjunct is
`card_ge_59`, the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. The only non-logical input is a `native_decide`
evaluation of the first 59 primes; the axioms are `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` together
with that `native_decide`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {P Q : Finset ℕ},
  (∀ p ∈ P, Nat.Prime p) →
    (∀ q ∈ Q, Nat.Prime q) →
      Q.Nonempty → 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (↑p)⁻¹) * ∑ q ∈ Q, (↑q)⁻¹ → 59 ≤ (P ∪ Q).card ∧ 4 * 10 ^ 112 ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, ↑p) ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)
$$
and
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).
$$
references: [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ P Q,
    0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧
      1 < P.card ∧
        1 < Q.card ∧ (↑P).Pairwise Nat.Coprime ∧ (↑Q).Pairwise Nat.Coprime ∧ 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (↑p)⁻¹) * ∑ q ∈ Q, (↑q)⁻¹

declarations.docstring: There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ P Q,
    0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧
      1 ∉ P ∪ Q ∧
        1 < P.card ∧
          1 < Q.card ∧ (↑P).Pairwise Nat.Coprime ∧ (↑Q).Pairwise Nat.Coprime ∧ 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (↑p)⁻¹) * ∑ q ∈ Q, (↑q)⁻¹

declarations.docstring:
Given any infinite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ there is a set $B$ of density $0$ such that $A+B$ contains all except finitely many integers.

Conjectured by Erdős and Straus. Proved by Lorentz [Lo54].
references: [erdosproblems.com/31](https://www.erdosproblems.com/31)
[Er56] Erdős, P., *Problems and results in additive number theory*. Colloque sur la Théorie des Nombres, Bruxelles, 1955 (1956), 127-137.
[Er59] Erdős, P., *Über einige Probleme der additiven Zahlentheorie*. Sammelband zu Ehren des 250. Geburtstages Leonhard Eulers (1959), 116-119.
[Er65b] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent advances and current problems in number theory*. Lectures on Modern Mathematics, Vol. III (1965), 196-244.

[Er73](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1973-21.pdf) Erdős, P., *Problems and results on combinatorial number theory*. A survey of combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971) (1973), 117-138.
[Lo54] Lorentz, G. G., *On a problem of additive number theory*. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1954), 838-841.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.Infinite → ∃ B, B.HasDensity 0 ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, n ∈ A + B

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist a constant `c > 0` such that, for any `K > 1`, whenever `A` is a sufficiently large
finite multiset of integers with $\sum_{n \in A} 1/n > K$ there exists some $S \subseteq A$ such that
$1 - \exp(-(c*K)) < \sum_{n \in S} 1/n \le 1$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/312](https://www.erdosproblems.com/312)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ c,
    0 < c ∧

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$ is a finite set with
$\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n} < 2$ then there is a partition $A=A_1 \sqcup A_2$
such that $\sum_{n \in A_i} \frac{1}{n} < 1$ for $i=1,2$?

This is not true in general, as shown by Sándor [Sa97].

The minimal counterexample is $\{2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15\}$, found by Tom Stobart.

This was formalized in Lean by Mehta.
references: [erdosproblems.com/316](https://www.erdosproblems.com/316)
[Sa97] Sándor, Csaba, On a problem of Erdős. J. Number Theory (1997), 203-210.
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ (A : Finset ℕ),
    0 ∉ A →
      1 ∉ A → ∑ n ∈ A, 1 / ↑n < 2 → ∃ A₁ A₂, Disjoint A₁ A₂ ∧ A = A₁ ∪ A₂ ∧ ∑ n ∈ A₁, 1 / ↑n < 1 ∧ ∑ n ∈ A₂, 1 / ↑n < 1

declarations.docstring:
This is not true in general, as shown by Sándor [Sa97], who observed that the proper divisors of
$120$ form a counterexample. More generally, Sándor shows that for any $n\geq 2$ there exists a
finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}\backslash\{1\}$ with $\sum_{k\in A}\frac{1}{k} < n$ and no
partition into $n$ parts each of which has $\sum_{k\in A_i}\frac{1}{k}<1$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/316](https://www.erdosproblems.com/316)
[Sa97] Sándor, Csaba, On a problem of Erdős. J. Number Theory (1997), 203-210.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  2 ≤ n →
    ∃ A,
      A.Nonempty ∧
        0 ∉ A ∧
          1 ∉ A ∧ ∑ k ∈ A, 1 / ↑k < ↑n ∧ ∀ (P : Finpartition A), P.parts.card = n → ∃ p ∈ P.parts, 1 ≤ ∑ n ∈ p, 1 / ↑n

declarations.docstring: This is not true if $A$ is a multiset, for example $2,3,3,5,5,5,5$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/316](https://www.erdosproblems.com/316)
[Sa97] Sándor, Csaba, On a problem of Erdős. J. Number Theory (1997), 203-210.
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ A,
  0 ∉ A ∧
    1 ∉ A ∧
      (Multiset.map (fun x => 1 / x) do
              let a ← A
              pure ↑a).sum <
          2 ∧
        ∀ (A₁ A₂ : Multiset ℕ),
          A = A₁ + A₂ →
            1 ≤
                (Multiset.map (fun x => 1 / x) do
                    let a ← A₁
                    pure ↑a).sum ∨
              1 ≤
                (Multiset.map (fun x => 1 / x) do
                    let a ← A₂
                    pure ↑a).sum

\frac{N}{\log N} \prod_{i=3}^{k} \log_i N \le R(N),
$$
valid for any $k \ge 4$ with $\log_k N \ge k$ and any $r \ge 1$ with $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$. (In these bounds $\log_i n$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.)

[BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erdős, P., _The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42.
[BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erdős, Paul, _Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II_. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.
references: [erdosproblems.com/321](https://www.erdosproblems.com/321)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (N k : ℕ), 4 ≤ k → ↑k ≤ Real.log^[k] ↑N → ↑N / Real.log ↑N * ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 3 k, Real.log^[i] ↑N ≤ ↑(Erdos321.R N)

declarations.docstring:
Let $R(N)$ be the maximal such size. Results of Bleicher and Erdős from [BlEr75] and [BlEr76b] imply that
$$
R(N) \le \frac{1}{\log 2} \log_r N \left( \frac{N}{\log N} \prod_{i=3}^{r} \log_i N \right),
$$
valid for any $k \ge 4$ with $\log_k N \ge k$ and any $r \ge 1$ with $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$. (In these bounds $\log_i n$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.)

[BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erdős, P., _The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42.
[BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erdős, Paul, _Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II_. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.
references: [erdosproblems.com/321](https://www.erdosproblems.com/321)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (N r : ℕ),
  1 ≤ r →
    1 ≤ Real.log^[2 * r] ↑N →
      ↑(Erdos321.R N) ≤ 1 / Real.log 2 * Real.log^[r] ↑N * ↑N / Real.log ↑N * ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 3 r, Real.log^[i] ↑N

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that $f_{k,k}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{1-\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$?

This would have significant applications to Waring's problem. Erdős and Graham describe this as
'unattackable by the methods at our disposal'.
references: [erdosproblems.com/323](https://www.erdosproblems.com/323)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ k ≥ 1, ∀ ε > 0, (fun x => ↑x ^ (1 - ε)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun x => ↑(Erdos323.f k k x)

declarations.docstring: Is it true that if $m < k$ then $f_{k,m}(x) \gg x^{m/k}$ for sufficiently large $x$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/323](https://www.erdosproblems.com/323)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ (k m : ℕ), 1 ≤ m → m < k → (fun x => ↑x ^ (↑m / ↑k)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun x => ↑(Erdos323.f k m x)

declarations.docstring:
The case $k=2$ was resolved by Landau, who showed $f_{2,2}(x) \sim \frac{cx}{\sqrt{\log x}}$ for
some constant $c>0$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/323](https://www.erdosproblems.com/323)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ c > 0, Asymptotics.IsEquivalent Filter.atTop (fun x => ↑(Erdos323.f 2 2 x)) fun x => c * ↑x / √(Real.log ↑x)

declarations.docstring: For $k>2$ it is not known if $f_{k,k}(x)=o(x)$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/323](https://www.erdosproblems.com/323)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ k > 2, (fun x => ↑(Erdos323.f k k x)) =o[Filter.atTop] fun x => ↑x

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ such that all the sums $f(a)+f(b)$ with
$a < b$ nonnegative integers are distinct?
references: [erdosproblems.com/324](https://www.erdosproblems.com/324)
declarations.type_pretty:
sorry ↔
  ∃ f,
    Set.InjOn
      (fun x =>
        match x with
        | (a, b) => Polynomial.eval (↑a) f + Polynomial.eval (↑b) f)
      {(a, b) | a < b}

declarations.docstring:
Probably $f(x) = x^5$ has the property that the sums $f(a)+f(b)$ with
$a < b$ nonnegative integers are distinct.
references: [erdosproblems.com/324](https://www.erdosproblems.com/324)
declarations.type_pretty:
Set.InjOn
  (fun x =>
    match x with
    | (a, b) => a ^ 5 + b ^ 5)
  {(a, b) | a < b}

declarations.docstring:
Writing $f_{k, 3}(x)$ for the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers,
is it true that $f_{k, 3}(x) \gg x ^ (3 / k)$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/325](https://www.erdosproblems.com/325)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ (k : ℕ), 3 ≤ k → (fun x => ↑x ^ (3 / ↑k)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun x => ↑(Erdos325.cardIsSumThreePowerBelow k x)

Writing $f_{k, 3}(x)$ for the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers,
is it even true that $f_{k, 3}(x) \gg_{\epsilon} x ^ (3 / k - \epsilon)$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/325](https://www.erdosproblems.com/325)

True ↔
  ∀ ε > 0,
    ∀ (k : ℕ), 3 ≤ k → (fun x => ↑x ^ (3 / ↑k - ε)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun x => ↑(Erdos325.cardIsSumThreePowerBelow k x)

declarations.docstring:
For $k = 3$, the best known is due to Wooley [Wo15]

declarations.docstring:
Let $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ be an additive basis of order 2.

Must there exist $B = \{b_1 < b_2 < \dots\} \subseteq A$ which is also a basis such that
$\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{b_k}{k^2}$ does not exist?
references: [erdosproblems.com/326](https://www.erdosproblems.com/326)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (A : Set ℕ),
    A.IsAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      ∃ b,
        StrictMono b ∧
          ∀ (n : ℕ),
            b n ∈ A ∧
              (Set.range b).IsAddBasis ∧ ∀ (x : ℝ), ¬Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(b n) / ↑n ^ 2) Filter.atTop (nhds x)

declarations.docstring: Erdős originally asked whether this was true with `A = B`, but this was disproved by Cassels.
references: [erdosproblems.com/326](https://www.erdosproblems.com/326)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ a,
  ∃ (_ : StrictMono a) (_ : (Set.range a).IsAddBasisOfOrder 2),
    ∃ x, ∃ (_ : 0 < x), Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(a n) / ↑n ^ 2) Filter.atTop (nhds x)

declarations.docstring:
Suppose $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and $C>0$ is such that $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\leq C$ for all
$n\in\mathbb{N}$. Can $A$ be partitioned into $t$ many subsets $A_1,\ldots,A_t$ (where
$t=t(C)$ depends only on $C$) such that $1_{A_i}\ast 1_{A_i}(n)<C$ for all $1\leq i\leq t$
and $n\in \mathbb{N}$?

The answer is no. Asked by Erdős and Newman. Nešetřil and Rödl [NeRo85] have shown the
answer is no for all $C$ (even if $t$ is also allowed to depend on $A$).

Erdős [Er80e] had previously shown the answer is no for $C=3,4$ and infinitely many other
values of $C$.

See also [774].
references: [erdosproblems.com/328](https://www.erdosproblems.com/328)
[Er80] Erdős, Paul, *A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory*. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
[Er80e] Erdős, P., *Some applications of Ramsey's theorem to additive number theory*. European J. Combin. (1980), 43-46.
[NeRo85] J. Nešetřil and V. Rödl, *Two proofs in combinatorial number theory*. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1985), 185-188.
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ (C : ℕ),
    0 < C →
      ∃ t,
        ∀ (A : Set ℕ),
          (∀ (n : ℕ), AdditiveCombinatorics.sumRep A n ≤ C) →
            ∃ P,
              ⋃ i, P i = A ∧
                Set.univ.PairwiseDisjoint P ∧ ∀ (i : Fin t) (n : ℕ), AdditiveCombinatorics.sumRep (P i) n < C

declarations.docstring:
**Erdős Problem 329.**
Let `A ⊆ ℕ` be a Sidon set. How large can
`lim sup_{N → ∞} |A ∩ {1,…,N}| / N^{1/2}`
be?
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: sSup {x | ∃ A, ∃ (_ : IsSidon A), Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A = x} = sorry

declarations.docstring:
If every finite Sidon set can be embedded in a perfect difference set modulo some $n > 0$,
then the maximum upper density of Sidon sets is 1. This is the implication stated on the source
page; the embedding hypothesis itself is known to be false by [Ha47] and [AlMi25].
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty:
(∀ (A : Finset ℕ), IsSidon ↑A → ∃ D n, ∃ (_ : n > 0), ↑A ⊆ D ∧ IsPerfectDifferenceSet D n) →
  sSup {x | ∃ A, ∃ (_ : IsSidon A), Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A = x} = 1

declarations.docstring:
Krückeberg ([Kr61]) exhibited an infinite Sidon set `A` with
`sidonUpperDensity A = 1 / Real.sqrt 2`, improving Erdős’ earlier
`1 / 2` lower bound.

[Kr61] Krückeberg, Fritz, $B\sb{2}$-Folgen und verwandte Zahlenfolgen. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1961), 53-60.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, IsSidon A ∧ Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A = 1 / √2

declarations.docstring:
Erdős proved that upper density `1 / 2` can be attained; in particular,
there exists a Sidon set whose upper density is *at least* `1 / 2`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, IsSidon A ∧ Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A ≥ 1 / 2

declarations.docstring:
Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved the upper bound of 1.

[ErTu41] Erdős, P. and Turán, P., On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems. J. London Math. Soc. (1941), 212-215.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), IsSidon A → Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A ≤ 1

declarations.docstring: It is possible to construct a Sidon set with positive density.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, IsSidon A ∧ 0 < Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A

declarations.docstring:
Let `A ⊆ ℕ` be a set such that every integer can be written as `n^2 + a`
for some `a` in `A` and `n ≥ 0`. What is the smallest possible value of
`lim sup n → ∞ |A ∩ {1, …, N}| / N^(1/2)`?
references: [erdosproblems.com/33](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33)
declarations.type_pretty: ⨅ A, Filter.limsup (fun N => ↑(↑A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / ↑√↑N) Filter.atTop = sorry

declarations.docstring: Erdos observed that this value is finite and > 1.
references: [erdosproblems.com/33](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, Erdos33.AdditiveBasisCondition A ∧ 1 < Filter.limsup (fun N => ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / √↑N) Filter.atTop

declarations.docstring:
The smallest possible value of `lim sup n → ∞ |A ∩ {1, …, N}| / N^(1/2)`
is at most `2φ^(5/2) ≈ 6.66`, with `φ` equal to the golden ratio. Proven by
Wouter van Doorn.
references: [erdosproblems.com/33](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33)
declarations.type_pretty: ⨅ A, Filter.limsup (fun N => ↑(↑A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / ↑√↑N) Filter.atTop ≤ ↑(2 * Real.goldenRatio ^ (5 / 2))

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist a minimal basis $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ with positive density
such that, for any $n \in A$, the (upper) density of integers which
cannot be represented without using $n$ is positive?
references: [erdosproblems.com/330](https://www.erdosproblems.com/330)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ A h,
    Erdos330.MinAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder A h ∧ A.HasPosDensity ∧ ∀ n ∈ A, (Erdos330.UnrepWithout A n h).HasPosDensity

declarations.docstring:
Let $A,B\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all large $N$$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg
N^{1/2}$$and$$\lvert B\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2}.$$
Is it true that there are infinitely many solutions to $a_1-a_2=b_1-b_2\neq 0$ with $a_1,a_2\in A$
and $b_1,b_2\in B$?

Ruzsa has observed that there is a simple counterexample: take $A$ to be the set of numbers whose
binary representation has only non-zero digits in even places, and $B$ similarly but with non-zero
digits only in odd places. It is easy to see $A$ and $B$ both grow like $\gg N^{1/2}$ and yet for
any $n\geq 1$ there is exactly one solution to $n=a+b$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$.

This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/331](https://www.erdosproblems.com/331)
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ (A B : Set ℕ),
    ((fun n => ↑n ^ (1 / 2)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑(Nat.count A n)) →
      ((fun n => ↑n ^ (1 / 2)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑(Nat.count B n)) →
        {(a₁, a₂, b₁, b₂) | a₁ ∈ A ∧ a₂ ∈ A ∧ b₁ ∈ B ∧ b₂ ∈ B ∧ a₁ ≠ a₂ ∧ a₁ + b₂ = a₂ + b₁}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
Ruzsa suggests that a non-trivial variant of this problem arises if one imposes the stronger
condition that $|A \cap \{1,\dots,N\}| \sim c_A N^{1/2}$ for some constant $c_A>0$, and similarly
for $B$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/331](https://www.erdosproblems.com/331)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (A B : Set ℕ),
    (∃ c_A > 0, Asymptotics.IsEquivalent Filter.atTop (fun n => ↑(Nat.count A n)) fun n => c_A * ↑n ^ (1 / 2)) →
      (∃ c_B > 0, Asymptotics.IsEquivalent Filter.atTop (fun n => ↑(Nat.count B n)) fun n => c_B * ↑n ^ (1 / 2)) →
        {(a₁, a₂, b₁, b₂) | a₁ ∈ A ∧ a₂ ∈ A ∧ b₁ ∈ B ∧ b₂ ∈ B ∧ a₁ ≠ a₂ ∧ a₁ + b₂ = a₂ + b₁}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $D(A)$ be the set of those numbers which occur infinitely often as
$a_1 - a_2$ with $a_1, a_2\in A$. What conditions on $A$ are sufficient to ensure $D(A)$ has bounded
gaps?

This is formalised here using the `answer(sorry)` mechanism. In order to solve this problem one
has to provide what the sufficient conditions are, and proof that they imply the desired condition.
If the condition is a solution to the problem is up to human judgement.
references: [erdosproblems.com/332](https://www.erdosproblems.com/332)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), sorry A → Erdos332.HasBoundedGaps (Erdos332.D_A A)

declarations.docstring:
For any permutation $\pi\in S_n$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $S(\pi)$ count the number of distinct consecutive sums, that is, sums of the shape $\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}\pi(i)$. Is it true that
$$
S(\pi) = o(n^2)
$$
for all $\pi\in S_n$?

Hegyvári [He86] gave a counterexample.
references: [erdosproblems.com/34](https://www.erdosproblems.com/34)
[Er77c] Erdős, Paul, *Problems and results on combinatorial number theory. III*. Number theory day (Proc. Conf., Rockefeller Univ., New York, 1976) (1977), 43-72.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[He86] Hegyvári, N., *On consecutive sums in sequences*. Acta Math. Hungar. (1986), 193--200.
[Ko15] Konieczny, J., *On consecutive sums in permutations*. arXiv:1504.07156 (2015).
declarations.type_pretty: False ↔ ∀ (c : ℝ), 0 < c → ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, ∀ (p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)), ↑(Erdos34.consecutiveSums n p).card < c * ↑n ^ 2

order of growth of $A$? Is it true that $|A \cap \{1, \ldots, N\}| \gg N^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$

declarations.docstring:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ be a finite set of integers and extend it to an infinite
sequence $\overline{A}=\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ by defining $a_{n+1}$ for $n \geq k$ to be
the least integer exceeding $a_n$ which is not of the form $a_i + a_j$ with $i,j \leq n$.
Is it true that the sequence of differences $a_{m+1}-a_m$ is eventually periodic?

This problem is discussed under Problem 7 on Green's open problems list.
references: [erdosproblems.com/341](https://www.erdosproblems.com/341)
[Ben Green's Open Problem 7](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.1)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (a : ℕ → ℤ),
    (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, IsLeast {x | a n < x ∧ x ∉ {x | ∃ i ≤ n, ∃ j ≤ n, a i + a j = x}} (a (n + 1))) →
      have d := fun i => a (i + 1) - a i;
      ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ (m : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, d (m + p) = d m

declarations.docstring: Does Ulam's sequence eventually have periodic differences? That is, is $a(n+1) - a(n)$ eventually periodic?

    Erdos342.IsUlamSequence a →
      have d := fun n => ↑(a (n + 1)) - ↑(a n);
      ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ (m : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, d (m + p) = d m

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that for every lacunary, strongly complete sequence `A` that is not complete whenever
infinitely many terms are removed from it, `lim A (n + 1) / A n = (1 + √5) / 2`?
references: [erdosproblems.com/346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346)
[Gr64d] Graham, R. L., A property of Fibonacci numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1964), 1-10.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980). -
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ {A : ℕ → ℕ},
    IsLacunary A →
      IsAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq A →
        (∀ B ⊆ Set.range A, B.Infinite → ¬IsAddComplete (Set.range A \ B)) →
          Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(A (n + 1)) / ↑(A n)) Filter.atTop (nhds ((1 + √5) / 2))

declarations.docstring:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also say that it is not hard to construct very irregular sequences
satisfying the aforementioned properties.
references: [erdosproblems.com/346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346)
[Gr64d] Graham, R. L., A property of Fibonacci numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1964), 1-10.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980). -
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ A,
  IsAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq A ∧
    (∀ B ⊆ Set.range A, B.Infinite → ¬IsAddComplete (Set.range A \ B)) ∧
      Filter.liminf (fun n => ↑(A (n + 1)) / 2) Filter.atTop = 1 ∧
        Filter.limsup (fun n => ↑(A (n + 1)) / ↑(A n)) Filter.atTop = ⊤

declarations.docstring: The sequence `f` is strongly complete, and this is proved in [Gr64d].
references: [erdosproblems.com/346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346)
[Gr64d] Graham, R. L., A property of Fibonacci numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1964), 1-10.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980). -

declarations.docstring: The sequence `f` is lacunary.

declarations.docstring:
The sequence `f` is not complete whenever infinitely many terms are removed from it, and this
is proved in [Gr64d].
references: [erdosproblems.com/346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346)
[Gr64d] Graham, R. L., A property of Fibonacci numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1964), 1-10.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980). -
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {B : Set ℕ}, B ⊆ Set.range Erdos346.f → B.Infinite → ¬IsAddComplete (Set.range Erdos346.f \ B)

declarations.docstring:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] remark that it is easy to see that if `A (n + 1) / A n > (1 + √5) / 2`
then the second property is automatically satisfied.
references: [erdosproblems.com/346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346)
[Gr64d] Graham, R. L., A property of Fibonacci numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1964), 1-10.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980). -
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {A : ℕ → ℕ},
  (∀ (n : ℕ), (1 + √5) / 2 * ↑(A n) < ↑(A (n + 1))) →
    ∀ {B : Set ℕ}, B ⊆ Set.range A → B.Infinite → ¬IsAddComplete (Set.range A \ B)

declarations.docstring:
Is there a sequence $A=\{a_1\leq a_2\leq \cdots\}$ of integers with
$$\lim \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=2$$
such that
$$P(A')= \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A'\textrm{ finite }\right\}$$
has density $1$ for every cofinite subsequence $A'$ of $A$?

This has been solved in the affirmative by ebarschkis in the comments (based on idea of Tao and
van Doorn, also in the comments).

Thos was formalized in Lean by Barschkis using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/347](https://www.erdosproblems.com/347)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ a,
    Monotone a ∧
      Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(a (n + 1)) / ↑(a n)) Filter.atTop (nhds 2) ∧
        ∀ (ι : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range ι)ᶜ.Finite → (subsetSums (Set.range (a ∘ ι))).HasDensity 1

declarations.docstring:
For what values of $0 \leq m < n$ is there a complete sequence
$A = \{a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots\}$ of integers such that
 1. $A$ remains complete after removing any $m$ elements, but
 2. $A$ is not complete after removing any $n$ elements.
references: [erdosproblems.com/348](https://www.erdosproblems.com/348)
declarations.type_pretty:
{x |
    ∃ m n,
      ∃ (_ : m < n),
        ∃ a,
          ∃ (_ : Monotone a) (_ :
            ∀ (s : Finset ℕ), s.card = m → IsAddComplete (Set.range (Function.updateFinset a s 0))) (_ :
            ∀ (t : Finset ℕ), t.card = n → ¬IsAddComplete (Set.range (Function.updateFinset a t 0))), (m, n) = x} =
  sorry

declarations.docstring:
For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively
complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős
Problem 349: it complements `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio`.

The proof is recorded via the `formal_proof` mechanism rather than written inline, as it exceeds
the repository's proof-length guideline.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℝ), 0 < t → 2 < α → ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α

declarations.docstring:
For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: every term
$\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ lies in the finite interval $[0, \lfloor t\rfloor]$ (since
$\alpha^n \le 1$), so every subset sum is bounded by the constant $\sum_{i \in [0,\lfloor t\rfloor]} i$,
and no large integer can be a subset sum. A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349,
complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℝ), 0 < t → 0 < α → α ≤ 1 → ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α

declarations.docstring:
It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all
for all $t>0$ and all $1 < \alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℝ), 0 < t → α ∈ Set.Ioo 1 ((1 + √5) / 2) → Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α

declarations.docstring:
**The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$.** For every $k$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the
sequence $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ is additively complete because at index $n = m + k$ it equals
the exact power $2^m$, so its range contains all powers of two, which already form an additively
complete set. Uses monotonicity `IsAddComplete.mono`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (k : ℕ), Erdos349.IsGoodPair (1 / 2 ^ k) 2

declarations.docstring:
For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete
(that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: {(t, α) | 0 < t ∧ 0 < α ∧ Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α} = sorry

declarations.docstring: Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are even infinitely often?
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | Even ⌊(3 / 2) ^ n⌋}.Infinite

Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are odd infinitely
often and even infinitely often?
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | Odd ⌊(3 / 2) ^ n⌋}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
**Binary expansion.** Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is
a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction:
subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)

declarations.docstring:
For any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha$
such that the sequence $\lfloor t_k\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete consists of at least $k$
disjoint line segments.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (k : ℕ),
  ∃ t ∈ Set.Ioo 0 1,
    ∃ ι,
      ↑k ≤ Set.univ.encard ∧
        ∃ I,
          (∀ (i : ι), 2 ≤ (I i).encard ∧ (I i).Nonempty ∧ IsConnected (I i)) ∧
            Pairwise (Function.onFun Disjoint I) ∧ ⋃ i, I i ⊆ {α | α > 0 ∧ Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α}

declarations.docstring:
**Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness.** For every integer base
$\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor =
t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every subset sum is too, but two consecutive large integers
cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial result
on Erdős Problem 349.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t : ℤ), 2 ≤ t → ∀ (α : ℤ), ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair ↑t ↑α

declarations.docstring:
**Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs.** For integers
$t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is
additively complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 2)$. Assembles the four partial results: $(1,2)$ is
good, $\alpha \le 1$ fails, $2 < \alpha$ fails (`alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair`), and integer
$t \ge 2$ fails.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℤ), 1 ≤ t → 1 ≤ α → (Erdos349.IsGoodPair ↑t ↑α ↔ t = 1 ∧ α = 2)

declarations.docstring:
**The pair $(1, 2)$ is good.** The powers of two $\lfloor 1\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^n$ form an
additively complete set: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum of distinct powers of two.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos349.IsGoodPair 1 2

[BeEr74] Benkoski, S. J. and Erdős, P., On weird and pseudoperfect numbers. Math. Comp. (1974), 617-623.
[HSS77] Hanson, F. and Steele, J. M. and Stenger, F., Distinct sums over subsets. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1977), 179-180.

∀ {M : Type u_1} [inst : AddCommMonoid M] [inst_1 : DecidableEq M] (A : Finset M),

[BeEr74] Benkoski, S. J. and Erdős, P., On weird and pseudoperfect numbers. Math. Comp. (1974), 617-623.
[HSS77] Hanson, F. and Steele, J. M. and Stenger, F., Distinct sums over subsets. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1977), 179-180.
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos350.DecidableDistinctSubsetSums {1, 2}

references: [erdosproblems.com/350](https://www.erdosproblems.com/350)
[BeEr74] Benkoski, S. J. and Erdős, P., On weird and pseudoperfect numbers. Math. Comp. (1974), 617-623.

declarations.docstring:
If `A ⊂ ℕ` is a finite set of integers all of whose subset sums are distinct then `∑ n ∈ A, 1/n < 2`.
Proved by Ryavec.

This was proved by Ryavec, who did not appear to ever publish the proof. Ryavec's proof is
reproduced in [BeEr74]. More generally, Ryavec's proof delivers that
$\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\leq 2-2^{1-\lvert A\rvert},$ with equality if and only if
$A=\{1,2,\ldots,2^k\}$.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/350](https://www.erdosproblems.com/350)
[BeEr74] Benkoski, S. J. and Erdős, P., On weird and pseudoperfect numbers. Math. Comp. (1974), 617-623.
[HSS77] Hanson, F. and Steele, J. M. and Stenger, F., Distinct sums over subsets. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1977), 179-180.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Finset ℕ), Erdos350.DecidableDistinctSubsetSums A → ∑ n ∈ A, 1 / ↑n < 2

declarations.docstring:
If `A ⊂ ℕ` is a finite set of integers all of whose subset sums are distinct then `∑ n ∈ A, 1/n^s < 1/(1 - 2^(-s))`, for any `s > 0`.
Proved by Hanson, Steele, and Stenger [HSS77].

We exlude here the case `s = 0`, because in the informal formulation then the right hand side is to be interpreted as `∞`, while the left hand side counts the elements in `A`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/350](https://www.erdosproblems.com/350)
[BeEr74] Benkoski, S. J. and Erdős, P., On weird and pseudoperfect numbers. Math. Comp. (1974), 617-623.
[HSS77] Hanson, F. and Steele, J. M. and Stenger, F., Distinct sums over subsets. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1977), 179-180.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Finset ℕ), Erdos350.DecidableDistinctSubsetSums A → ∀ (s : ℝ), 0 < s → ∑ n ∈ A, (1 / ↑n) ^ s < 1 / (1 - 2 ^ (-s))

declarations.docstring:
Let $p(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a non-constant rational polynomial with positive leading
coefficient. Is it true that $$A=\{ p(n)+1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$$ is strongly complete,
in the sense that, for any finite set $B$,
$$\left\{\sum_{a \in X} a : X \subseteq A \setminus B, X \textrm{ is finite}\right\}$$
contains all sufficiently large integers?
references: [erdosproblems.com/351](https://www.erdosproblems.com/351)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ (P : Polynomial ℚ), 0 < P.natDegree → 0 < P.leadingCoeff → Erdos351.HasCompleteImage P

declarations.docstring:
Let $p(x) = x \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. It has been shown that
$$A=\{ p(n)+1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$$
is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$,
$$\left\{\sum_{a \in X} a : X \subseteq A \setminus B, X \textrm{ is finite}\right\}$$
contains all sufficiently large integers.
references: [erdosproblems.com/351](https://www.erdosproblems.com/351)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos351.HasCompleteImage Polynomial.X

declarations.docstring:
Is there some $c > 0$ such that every measurable $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of measure $\geq c$
contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?
references: [erdosproblems.com/352](https://www.erdosproblems.com/352)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ c > 0,
    ∀ (A : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
      MeasurableSet A →
        ↑(MeasureTheory.volume A) ≥ ↑c →
          ∃ t,
            (∀ (p : Fin 3), t.points p ∈ A) ∧ EuclideanGeometry.triangle_area (t.points 0) (t.points 1) (t.points 2) = 1

declarations.docstring:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a measurable set with infinite measure. Must $A$ contain the
vertices of an isosceles trapezoid of area $1$? What about an isosceles triangle, or a
right-angled triangle, or a cyclic quadrilateral, or a convex polygon with congruent sides?

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

This statement formalizes the leading question, for isosceles trapezoids; the remaining
configurations are given as variants below. The area of a polygon is taken to be the Lebesgue
measure of the convex hull of its vertices.
references: [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
[Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
[Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*. arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
[KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
[Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (A : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
    MeasurableSet A →
      MeasureTheory.volume A = ⊤ →
        ∃ a ∈ A,
          ∃ b ∈ A,
            ∃ c ∈ A,
              ∃ d ∈ A,
                EuclideanGeometry.IsIsoscelesTrapezoid a b c d ∧ MeasureTheory.volume ((convexHull ℝ) {a, b, c, d}) = 1

declarations.docstring:
The answer is negative for convex polygons with congruent sides: Kovač and Predojević
[KoPr24] prove that there exists a set of infinite measure such that every convex polygon
with congruent sides and all vertices in the set has area $<1$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
[Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
[Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*. arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
[KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
[Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ A,
  MeasurableSet A ∧
    MeasureTheory.volume A = ⊤ ∧
      ∀ (n : ℕ) (v : Fin (n + 3) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)),
        EuclideanGeometry.IsCcwConvexPolygon v →
          (∀ (i : Fin (n + 3)), v i ∈ A) →
            (∀ (i : Fin (n + 3)), dist (v i) (v (i + 1)) = dist (v 0) (v 1)) →
              MeasureTheory.volume ((convexHull ℝ) (Set.range v)) < 1

declarations.docstring:
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
cyclic quadrilateral of area $1$.

Kovač and Predojević [KoPr24] have proved that this is true for cyclic quadrilaterals - that
is, every set with infinite measure contains four distinct points on a circle such that the
quadrilateral determined by these four points has area $1$. The quadrilateral determined by
four distinct concyclic points is their convex hull.
references: [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
[Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
[Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*. arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
[KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
[Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (A : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
  MeasurableSet A →
    MeasureTheory.volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ Q ⊆ A, Q.ncard = 4 ∧ EuclideanGeometry.Cospherical Q ∧ MeasureTheory.volume ((convexHull ℝ) Q) = 1

declarations.docstring:
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of an
isosceles triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
references: [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
[Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
[Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*. arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
[KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
[Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (A : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
  MeasurableSet A →
    MeasureTheory.volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A, IsIsosceles a b c ∧ MeasureTheory.volume ((convexHull ℝ) {a, b, c}) = 1

right-angled triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate

[Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
[Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*. arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
[KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).

declarations.docstring:
Let $\alpha,\beta\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that $\alpha/\beta$ is irrational. Is
$$\{ \lfloor \alpha\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma\alpha\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma^2\alpha\rfloor,\ldots\}\cup
\{ \lfloor \beta\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma\beta\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma^2\beta\rfloor,\ldots\}$$ complete?
references: [erdosproblems.com/354](https://www.erdosproblems.com/354)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ α > 0, ∀ β > 0, Irrational (α / β) → IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (Erdos354.FloorMultiples.interleave α β 2)

declarations.docstring:
Let $\alpha,\beta\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that $\alpha/\beta$ is irrational. Is
$$\{ \lfloor \alpha\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma\alpha\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma^2\alpha\rfloor,\ldots\}\cup
\{ \lfloor \beta\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma\beta\rfloor,\lfloor \gamma^2\beta\rfloor,\ldots\}$$ complete?
references: [erdosproblems.com/354](https://www.erdosproblems.com/354)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ γ ∈ Set.Ioo 1 2,
    ∀ α > 0, ∀ β > 0, Irrational (α / β) → IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (Erdos354.FloorMultiples.interleave α β 2)

declarations.docstring:
Is there a lacunary sequence $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (so that $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ and
there exists some $\lambda > 1$ such that $a_{n+1}/a_n\geq \lambda$ for all $n\geq 1$) such that
$$\left\{ \sum_{a\in A'}\frac{1}{a} : A'\subseteq A\textrm{ finite}\right\}$$
contain all rationals in some open interval?

Bleicher and Erdős conjectured the answer is no.

In fact the answer is yes, with any lacunarity constant $\lambda\in (1,2)$ (though not $\lambda=2$),
as proved by van Doorn and Kova\v{c} [DoKo25].

This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/355](https://www.erdosproblems.com/355)
[DoKo25] W. van Doorn and V. Kovač, Lacunary sequences whose reciprocal sums represent all rationals in an interval. arXiv:2509.24971 (2025).
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ A,
    IsLacunary A ∧
      ∃ u v, u < v ∧ ∀ (q : ℚ), ↑q ∈ Set.Ioo u v → q ∈ {x | ∃ A', ∃ (_ : ↑A' ⊆ Set.range A), ∑ a ∈ A', 1 / ↑a = x}

declarations.docstring:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of
solutions to $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.$$
Is there such an $A$ for which $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$?

Tao [Ta26] constructed such a sequence with $f(n) \gg \log n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
[Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ Filter.Tendsto (Erdos358.f A) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop

declarations.docstring:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of
solutions to $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.$$
Is there an $A$ such that $f(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$?

This also follows from Tao's construction with $f(n) \gg \log n$ [Ta26].
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
[Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, 2 ≤ Erdos358.f A n

$$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$$ such that the sum has at least two terms, then for all $n$ we have
$1 \leq g(n)$ for sufficiently large $n$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)

declarations.docstring: When $A_n = n$, the function $f$ defined above counts the number of odd divisors of $n$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
[Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)

declarations.docstring:
This example calculates the value of $M 1$. The set is $\{1, 2\}$, so the only partition is
$A = \{1\}, B = \{2\}$ (or vice versa). The possible differences are $1 - 2 = -1$ and $2 - 1 = 1$.
The `Overlap` for $k=-1$ is 1 (if $A=\{1\}, B=\{2\}$) and for $k=1$ also 1 (if $A=\{2\}, B=\{1\}$ ).
The `MaxOverlap` is $1$, since the `Overlap` is $0$ for other $k$.
Thus, $M 1 = 1$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/36](https://www.erdosproblems.com/36)
[Wikipedial: Minimum overlap problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_overlap_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos36.M 1 = 1

declarations.docstring:
For $n = 2$, the set is $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. The balanced partition $A = \{1, 4\}, B = \{2, 3\}$
has all four pairwise differences ($\pm 1, \pm 2$) distinct, so `MaxOverlap = 1`.
Any balanced partition has both pieces nonempty, so `MaxOverlap \geq 1`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/36](https://www.erdosproblems.com/36)
[Wikipedial: Minimum overlap problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_overlap_problem)

declarations.docstring:
Let $c > 0$ and $n$ be some large integer. What is the size of the largest set
$A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, \lfloor c n \rfloor\}$ such that $n$ is not a sum of a subset of $A$?
Does this depend on $n$ in an irregular way?
references: [erdosproblems.com/361](https://www.erdosproblems.com/361)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (c : ℝ),
  0 < c →
    ∀ (A : ℕ → ℕ),
      (∀ (c n : ℕ), A n = {B ∈ (Finset.Icc 1 ⌊c * n⌋₊).powerset | n ≠ ∑ a ∈ B, a}.sup Finset.card) →
        (fun n => ↑(A n)) =O[Filter.atTop] sorry

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that there are only finitely many collections of disjoint intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ of size $\lvert I_i\rvert \geq 4$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ such that$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}\prod_{m\in I_i}m$$is a square?

This is false: Ulas [Ul05] constructed infinitely many such collections.
references: [erdosproblems.com/363](https://www.erdosproblems.com/363)
[BaBe07] Bauer, Mark and Bennett, Michael A., *On a question of Erd\H{o}s and Graham*. Enseign. Math. (2) (2007), 259--264.
[BeVL12] Bennett, Michael A. and Van Luijk, Ronald, *Squares from blocks of consecutive integers: a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham*. Indag. Math. (N.S.) (2012), 123--127.
[Ul05] Ulas, Maciej, *On products of disjoint blocks of consecutive integers*. Enseign. Math. (2) (2005), 331--334.
declarations.type_pretty: False ↔ {S | Erdos363.IsValidCollection S}.Finite

declarations.docstring: There is no consecutive triple of powerful numbers.
references: [erdosproblems.com/364](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364)
declarations.type_pretty: ¬∃ n, n.Powerful ∧ (n + 1).Powerful ∧ (n + 2).Powerful

declarations.docstring:
Erdős [Er76d] conjectured a stronger statement: if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number,
then $n_{k+2} - n_k > n_k^c$ for some constant $c > 0$.

[Er76d] Erdős, P., Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics (Univ. Manitoba, Winnipeg, Man., 1975) (1976), 25-44.
references: [erdosproblems.com/364](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c,
  ∃ (_ : c > 0), ∀ (k : ℕ), ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Powerful (k + 2)) - ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Powerful k) > ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Powerful k) ^ c

declarations.docstring:
There is no quadruple of powerful numbers, since at least one of the four numbers must be
$2 \pmod{4}$, which cannot be powerful (since $2$ divides it, but $2^2$ does not).
references: [erdosproblems.com/364](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364)
declarations.type_pretty: ¬∃ n, n.Powerful ∧ (n + 1).Powerful ∧ (n + 2).Powerful ∧ (n + 3).Powerful

declarations.docstring: Are there any $2$-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is $3$-full?
references: [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ n > 0, Nat.Full 2 n ∧ Nat.Full 3 (n + 1)

declarations.docstring: Are there infinitely many 3-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is 2-full?
references: [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | Nat.Full 3 n ∧ Nat.Full 2 (n + 1)}.Infinite

declarations.docstring: Are there any consecutive pairs of $3$-full integers?
references: [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ n > 0, Nat.Full 3 n ∧ Nat.Full 3 (n + 1)

declarations.docstring: Note that $8$ is $3$-full and $9$ is 2-full.
references: [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ n > 0, Nat.Full 3 n ∧ Nat.Full 2 (n + 1)

declarations.docstring:
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the largest prime factor of $n$ is $< n^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and
the largest prime factor of $n + 1$ is $< (n + 1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Steinerberger has pointed out this problem has a trivial solution.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/370](https://www.erdosproblems.com/370)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | ↑n.maxPrimeFac < √↑n ∧ ↑(n + 1).maxPrimeFac < √(↑n + 1)}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. Show that the set of $n$
with $P(n+1) > P(n)$ has density $\frac{1}{2}$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/371](https://www.erdosproblems.com/371)
declarations.type_pretty: {n | (n + 1).maxPrimeFac > n.maxPrimeFac}.HasDensity (1 / 2)

declarations.docstring:
Show that the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has
only finitely many solutions.
references: [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos373.S.Finite

declarations.docstring:
Hickerson conjectured the largest solution the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with
`n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, is `16!=14!5!2!`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)

declarations.docstring:
Show that if `P(n(n+1)) / log n → ∞` where `P(m)` denotes the largest prime factor of `m`, then
the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has only
finitely many solutions.
references: [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)
declarations.type_pretty: Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(n * (n + 1)).maxPrimeFac / Real.log ↑n) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop → Erdos373.S.Finite

declarations.docstring:
Show that if `P(n(n−1)) > 4 log n` for large enough `n`, where `P(m)` denotes the
largest prime factor of `m`, then the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with
`n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has only finitely many solutions.
references: [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)
declarations.type_pretty: (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, 4 * Real.log ↑n < ↑(n * (n - 1)).maxPrimeFac) → Erdos373.S.Finite

declarations.docstring:
Surányi was the first to conjecture that the only non-trivial solution to `a!b!=n!`
is `6!7!=10!`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)
declarations.type_pretty: {(n, a, b) | n.factorial = a.factorial * b.factorial ∧ 1 < n ∧ 1 < a ∧ 1 < b ∧ b ≤ a ∧ a + 1 ≠ n} = {(10, 7, 6)}

declarations.docstring: Is `Erdos375Prop` true?
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ Erdos375.Erdos375Prop

declarations.docstring:
If `Erdos375Prop` is true, then `(n + 1).nth Prime - n.nth Prime < (n.nth Prime) ^ (1 / 2 - c)`
for some `c > 0`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty:
Erdos375.Erdos375Prop →
  ∃ c > 0,
    ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
      ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1)) - ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) < ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) ^ (1 / 2 - c)

declarations.docstring:
It is easy to see that for any `n ≥ 1` and `k ≤ 2`, if `n + 1, ..., n + k` are all composite,
then there are distinct primes `p₁, ... pₖ` such that `pᵢ ∣ n + i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ k`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ n ≥ 1,
  ∀ k ≤ 2,
    (∀ i < k, ¬Nat.Prime (n + i + 1)) → ∃ p, Function.Injective p ∧ ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (p i) ∧ p i ∣ n + ↑i + 1

declarations.docstring: In particular, if `Erdos375Prop` is true, then Legendre's conjecture is asymptotically true.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos375.Erdos375Prop → ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring:
There exists a constant `c > 0` such that for all `n`, if
`k < c * (log n / (log (log n))) ^ 3 → (∀ i < k, ¬ (n + i + 1).Prime)`, then
there are distinct primes `p₁, ... pₖ` such that `pᵢ ∣ n + i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ k`. This is proved
in [RST75]. There is no need to only consider sufficiently large `n` because one can always take
`c` small enough so that `k < c * (log n / (log (log n))) ^ 3` implies that `k = 0` until `n` is
large.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c > 0,
  ∀ (n k : ℕ),
    ↑k < c * (Real.log ↑n / Real.log (Real.log ↑n)) ^ 3 →
      (∀ i < k, ¬Nat.Prime (n + i + 1)) → ∃ p, Function.Injective p ∧ ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (p i) ∧ p i ∣ n + ↑i + 1

declarations.docstring: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that ${2n\choose n}$ is coprime to $105$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/376](https://www.erdosproblems.com/376)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | n.centralBinom.Coprime 105}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75] have shown that, for any two odd primes $p$ and $q$,
there are infinite many $n$ such that ${2n\choose n}$ is coprime to $pq$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/376](https://www.erdosproblems.com/376)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {p q : ℕ}, Nat.Prime p → Odd p → Nat.Prime q → Odd q → {n | n.centralBinom.Coprime (p * q)}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
Is there some absolute constant $C > 0$ such that
$$
  \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p} \leq C
$$
for all $n$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ C > 0, ∀ (n : ℕ), Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n ≤ C

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then for almost all integers $f(m) = \gamma_0 + o(1)$.

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (γ₀ : ℝ),
  γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), Real.log (↑k + 2) / 2 ^ (k + 2) →
    ∃ o,
      ∃ (_ : Filter.Tendsto o Filter.atTop (nhds 0)),
        ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.cofinite, Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n = γ₀ + o n

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then
$$
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x} f(n) = \gamma_0
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (γ₀ : ℝ),
  γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), Real.log (↑k + 2) / 2 ^ (k + 2) →
    Filter.Tendsto (fun x => 1 / ↑x * ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 x, Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n) Filter.atTop
      (nhds γ₀)

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then
$$
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x} f(n)^2 = \gamma_0^2
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (γ₀ : ℝ),
  γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), Real.log (↑k + 2) / 2 ^ (k + 2) →
    Filter.Tendsto (fun x => 1 / ↑x * ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 x, Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n ^ 2) Filter.atTop
      (nhds (γ₀ ^ 2))

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
then there is some constant $c < 1$ such that for all large $n$
$$
  f(n) \leq c \log\log n.
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ c < 1, ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n ≤ c * Real.log (Real.log ↑n)

declarations.docstring:
Let $S(n)$ denote the largest integer such that, for all $1 ≤ k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by $p^S(n)$ for some prime $p$ (depending on $k$).Then
$\limsup S(n) = \infty$.

This was formalized in Lean by Tao.
references: [erdosproblems.com/379](https://www.erdosproblems.com/379)
declarations.type_pretty: Filter.limsup (fun n => ↑(Erdos379.S n)) Filter.atTop = ⊤

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ which is not an additive basis,
but is such that for every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$
and every $N$ there exists $b \in B$ such that
$$
  \lvert (A \cup (A+b)) \cap \{1, \ldots, N\} \rvert \geq (\alpha + f(\alpha)) N
$$
where $f(\alpha) > 0$ for $0 < \alpha < 1$?

Note: here Erdős seems to use a slightly weaker notion of an additive basis (see [Er56] at the top
of page 135). In particular, for this problem, a set is an additive basis of order $k$ if every
natural number can be written as a sum of _at most_ $k$ elements of the set, rather than as a sum of
_precisely_ $k$ elements.

A positive [solution](https://github.com/spicylemonade/erdos-38) was given by GPT 5.5 Pro
(prompted by gebyjaff, cleanup by Liam Price); in fact a sparse random set $B$ has this property,
with $f(\alpha)\gg \alpha (1-\alpha)^2$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/38](https://www.erdosproblems.com/38)
[Er56](Erdős, P., Problems and results in additive number theory. Colloque sur la Théorie des Nombres, Bruxelles, 1955 (1956), 127-137.)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ B,
    ¬B.IsWeakAddBasis ∧
      ∃ f,
        (∀ (α : ℝ), 0 < α → α < 1 → f α > 0) ∧
          ∀ (A : Set ℕ) (N : ℕ),
            have α := schnirelmannDensity A;
            ∃ b ∈ B, ↑(Set.Ioc 0 N ∩ (A ∪ (A + {b}))).ncard ≥ (α + f α) * ↑N

declarations.docstring:

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that for every $n \geq 1$ there is a $k$ such that

for all $\varepsilon > 0$?

True ↔

declarations.docstring:
Let $A(n)$ denote the least value of $t$ such that
$$
  n! = a_1 \cdots a_t
$$
with $a_1 \leq \cdots \leq a_t\leq n^2$. Then
$$
  A(n) = \frac{n}{2} - \frac{n}{2\log n} + o\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right).
$$
references: [erdosproblems.com/392](https://www.erdosproblems.com/392)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (A : ℕ → ℕ),
  (∀ n > 0,
      IsLeast {x | ∃ t, ∃ (_ : ∃ a, n.factorial = ∏ i, a i ∧ Monotone a ∧ a (Fin.last t) ≤ n ^ 2), t + 1 = x} (A n)) →
    (fun n => ↑(A n) - ↑n / 2 + ↑n / (2 * Real.log ↑n)) =o[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑n / Real.log ↑n

declarations.docstring:
Cambie has observed that a positive answer follows from the result above with $a_t \leq n$, simply
by pairing variables together, e.g. taking $a'_i = a_{2i-1}a_{2i}$ (and the lower bound follows from
Stirling's approximation).
references: [erdosproblems.com/392](https://www.erdosproblems.com/392)
declarations.type_pretty:
(∀ (A : ℕ → ℕ),
    (∀ n > 0,
        IsLeast {x | ∃ t, ∃ (_ : ∃ a, n.factorial = ∏ i, a i ∧ Monotone a ∧ a (Fin.last t) ≤ n ^ 2), t + 1 = x} (A n)) →
      (fun n => ↑(A n) - ↑n / 2 + ↑n / (2 * Real.log ↑n)) =o[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑n / Real.log ↑n) →
  ∀ (A : ℕ → ℕ),
    (∀ n > 0,
        IsLeast {x | ∃ t, ∃ (_ : ∃ a, n.factorial = ∏ i, a i ∧ Monotone a ∧ a (Fin.last t) ≤ n), t + 1 = x} (A n)) →
      (fun n => ↑(A n) - ↑n + ↑n / Real.log ↑n) =o[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑n / Real.log ↑n

declarations.docstring:
If we change the condition to $a_t \leq n$ it can be shown that
$$
  A(n) = n - \frac{n}{\log n} + o\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)
$$
references: [erdosproblems.com/392](https://www.erdosproblems.com/392)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (A : ℕ → ℕ),
  (∀ n > 0, IsLeast {x | ∃ t, ∃ (_ : ∃ a, n.factorial = ∏ i, a i ∧ Monotone a ∧ a (Fin.last t) ≤ n), t + 1 = x} (A n)) →
    (fun n => ↑(A n) - ↑n + ↑n / Real.log ↑n) =o[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑n / Real.log ↑n

declarations.docstring: Is it true that $\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{x^2}{(\log x)^c}$ for some $c>0$?

[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

True ↔
  ∀ k ≥ 2,
    (fun x => ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊, ↑(Erdos394.t (k + 1) n)) =o[Filter.atTop] fun x =>
      ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊, ↑(Erdos394.t k n)

They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$ and also ask whether, for infinitely many $n$,
$t_k(n!)< t_{k-1}(n!)-1$ for all $1\leq k < n$.

and Hall [ErHa78], who proved that in fact

  ↑x ^ 2 * (Real.log (Real.log (Real.log ↑x)) / Real.log (Real.log ↑x))

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that for every $k$ there exists $n$ such that
$$\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(n-i) \mid \binom{2n}{n}?$$
references: [erdosproblems.com/396](https://www.erdosproblems.com/396)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ (k : ℕ), ∃ n, n.descFactorial (k + 1) ∣ n.centralBinom

declarations.docstring:
Are there only finitely many solutions to
$$
  \prod_i \binom{2m_i}{m_i}=\prod_j \binom{2n_j}{n_j}
$$
with the $m_i,n_j$ distinct?

Somani, using ChatGPT, has given a negative answer. In fact, for any $a\geq 2$, if $c=8a^2+8a+1$,
$\binom{2a}{a}\binom{4a+4}{2a+2}\binom{2c}{c}= \binom{2a+2}{a+1}\binom{4a}{2a}\binom{2c+2}{c+1}.$
Further families of solutions are given in the comments by SharkyKesa.

This was earlier asked about in a [MathOverflow] question, in response to which Elkies also gave an
alternative construction which produces solutions - at the moment it is not clear whether Elkies'
argument gives infinitely many solutions (although Bloom believes that it can).

This was formalized in Lean by Wu using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/397](https://www.erdosproblems.com/397)
[MathOverflow] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/138209/product-of-central-binomial-coefficients)
declarations.type_pretty: False ↔ {(M, N) | Disjoint M N ∧ ∏ i ∈ M, i.centralBinom = ∏ j ∈ N, j.centralBinom}.Finite

declarations.docstring:
**Brocard's Problem**
Does $n! + 1 = m^2$ have integer solutions other than $n = 4, 5, 7$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/398](https://www.erdosproblems.com/398)
[Wikipedia: Brocard's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brocard%27s_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: sorry ↔ {n | ∃ m, n.factorial + 1 = m ^ 2} = {4, 5, 7}

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that there are no solutions to `n! = x^k ± y^k` with `x,y,n ∈ ℕ`, `x*y > 1`, and
`k > 2`?

The answer is no: Jonas Barfield found the counterexample `10! = 48^4 - 36^4` (equivalently,
`10! + 36^4 = 48^4`).

This is discussed in problem D2 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

This was formalized in Lean by Lu using Codex.
references: [erdosproblems.com/399](https://www.erdosproblems.com/399)
[Br32] Breusch, Robert, Zur Verallgemeinerung des Bertrandschen Postulates, da\ss zwischen $x$ und 2 $x$ stets Primzahlen liegen. Math. Z. (1932), 505--526.
[ErOb37] Erdős, P. and Obláth, R., \"Über diophantische Gleichungen der Form $n!=x^p+y^p$ und $n!\pmd m!=x^p$. Acta Litt. ac Sci. Reg. Univ. Hung. Fr.-Jos., Sect. Sci. Math. (1937), 241-255.
[Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
[PoSh73] Pollack, Richard M. and Shapiro, Harold N., The next to last case of a factorial diophantine equation. Comm. Pure Appl. Math. (1973), 313-325.
declarations.type_pretty: False ↔ ¬∃ n x y k, 1 < x * y ∧ 2 < k ∧ (n.factorial = x ^ k + y ^ k ∨ n.factorial + y ^ k = x ^ k)

declarations.docstring:
Cambie has also observed that considerations modulo $8$ rule out any solutions to $n!=x^4+y^4$ with
$(x,y)=1$ and $xy>1$.

Erdős and Obláth observed that the Bertrand-style fact (first proved by Breusch [Br32]) that, if
$q_i$ is the sequence of primes congruent to $3\pmod{4}$ then $q_{i+1}<2q_i$ except for $q_1=3$,
together with Fermat's theorem on the sums of two squares implies that the only solution to
$n!=x^2+y^2$ is $6!=12^2+24^2$.

Erdős-Turán conjecture, see Erdõs Problem 28,

declarations.docstring: Can one show that $\sum_{n\leq x}g_k(n) \sim c_k x\log x$ for some constant $c_k$?

declarations.docstring:
Prove that, for any finite set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$, there exist $a, b\in A$ such
that
$$
  \gcd(a, b)\leq a/|A|.
$$
references: [erdosproblems.com/402](https://www.erdosproblems.com/402)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Finset ℕ), 0 ∉ A → A.Nonempty → ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ↑(a.gcd b) ≤ ↑a / ↑A.card

declarations.docstring:
A conjecture of Graham [Gr70], who also conjectured that (assuming $A$ itself
has no common divisor) the only cases where equality is achieved are when
$A = \{1, \dots, n\}$ or $A = \{L/1, \dots, L/n\}$ (where $L = \operatorname{lcm}(1, \dots, n)$) or
$A = \{2, 3, 4, 6\}$.
Note: The source [BaSo96] mentioned on the Erdős page makes it clear what
quantifiers to use for "where equality is achieved". See Theorem 1.1 there.

TODO(firsching): Consider if we should have the other direction here as well or
an iff statement.
references: [erdosproblems.com/402](https://www.erdosproblems.com/402)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (A : Finset ℕ),
  0 ∉ A →
    A.Nonempty →
      A.gcd id = 1 →
        (∀ a ∈ A, ∀ b ∈ A, ↑a / ↑A.card ≤ ↑(a.gcd b)) →
          A = Finset.Icc 1 A.card ∨
            A = Finset.image (fun x => (Finset.Icc 1 A.card).lcm id / x) (Finset.Icc 1 A.card) ∨ A = {2, 3, 4, 6}

declarations.docstring:
Proved for all sufficiently large sets (including the sharper version which
characterises the case of equality) independently by Szegedy [Sz86] and
Zaharescu [Za87]. The following is taken from [Sz86].

There exists an effectively computable $n_0$ with the following properties:
(i) if $n \ge n_0$ and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are distinct natural numbers then
$\max_{i, j} \frac{a_i}{(a_i, a_j)} \ge n$.
(ii) If equality holds then the system $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ is either of the
type $\{k, 2k, \dots, nk\}$ or of the type
$\left\{\frac{k}{1}, \frac{k}{2}, \dots, \frac{k}{n}\right\}$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/402](https://www.erdosproblems.com/402)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
  ∀ (A : Finset ℕ),
    A.card = n →
      0 ∉ A →
        (n ≤ (A ×ˢ A).sup fun x => x.1 / x.1.gcd x.2) ∧
          ((n = (A ×ˢ A).sup fun x => x.1 / x.1.gcd x.2) ↔
            ∃ k > 0,
              A = Finset.image (fun x => k * x) (Finset.Icc 1 n) ∨
                A = Finset.image (fun x => k * (Finset.Icc 1 n).lcm id / x) (Finset.Icc 1 n))

declarations.docstring:
Does the equation
$$2^m=a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$$
with $a_1<a_2<\cdots <a_k$ have only finitely many solutions?

Asked by Burr and Erdős. Frankl and Lin [Li76] independently showed that the answer is yes, and
the largest solution is
$$2^7=2!+3!+5!.$$
In fact Lin showed that the largest power of $2$ which can divide a sum of distinct factorials
containing $2$ is $2^{254}$, and that there are only 5 solutions to $3^m=a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$
(when $m=0,1,2,3,6$).

See also [404].

A solution is encoded below as a pair $(m, s)$ where $s$ is the finite set
$\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k\}$ of positive integers, so the distinctness of the $a_i$ is
given by set membership. The empty set contributes no solutions since $2^m \geq 1 > 0$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/403](https://www.erdosproblems.com/403)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
[Li76] Lin, S., *On two problems of Erdős concerning sums of distinct factorials*. Bell Laboratories internal memorandum (1960).
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {p | (∀ a ∈ p.2, 0 < a) ∧ 2 ^ p.1 = ∑ a ∈ p.2, a.factorial}.Finite

references: [erdosproblems.com/41](https://www.erdosproblems.com/41)

  Erdos41.NtupleCondition A 3 →
    A.Infinite → Filter.liminf (fun N => ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / ↑N ^ (1 / 3)) Filter.atTop = 0

Is it true that $\lim_{k → ∞} σ_k(n)^{\frac 1 k} = ∞$?

This is problem (iii) from
Erdos, Granville, Pomerance, Spiro
"On the normal behavior of the iterates of some arithmetical functions"
(page 169 of the book "Analytic Number Theory", 1990).
references: [erdosproblems.com/410](https://www.erdosproblems.com/410)

declarations.docstring:
Let `V(x)` count the number of `n≤x` such that `ϕ(m)=n` is solvable.
Erdős proved V(x)=x(logx)^(−1+o(1)).
Ref: Erdős, P., _On the normal number of prime factors of $p-1$ and some related problems concerning Euler's $\varphi$-function._
references: [erdosproblems.com/416](https://www.erdosproblems.com/416)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ f, f =o[Filter.atTop] 1 ∧ ∀ᶠ (x : ℝ) in Filter.atTop, Erdos416.V x = x * Real.log x ^ (-1 + f x)

declarations.docstring:
Let `V(x)` count the number of `n≤x` such that `ϕ(m)=n` is solvable.
`V(x) ≍ x/log x*e^(C_1*(log log log x − log log log log x)^2+C_2 log log log x − C_3 log log log log x)`
Ref: Ford, Kevin, _The distribution of totients_.

declarations.docstring:
Are there infinitely many integers not of the form $n - \phi(n)$?

Asked by Erdős and Sierpiński. Numbers not of the form we call non-cototients.

Browkin and Schinzel [BrSc95] provided an affirmative answer to this question, proving that any
integer of the shape $2^{k}\cdot 509203$ for $k\geq 1$ is a non-cototient.

This is discussed in problem B36 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/418](https://www.erdosproblems.com/418)
[BaLu05] Banks, William D. and Luca, Florian, Nonaliquots and {R}obbins numbers. Colloq. Math. (2005), 27--32.

[ChZh11] Chen, Yong-Gao and Zhao, Qing-Qing, Nonaliquot numbers. Publ. Math. Debrecen (2011), 439--442.
[Er73b] Erdős, P., \"Über die Zahlen der Form $\sigma (n)-n$ und $n-\phi(n)$. Elem. Math. (1973), 83-86.

[PoPo16] Pollack, Paul and Pomerance, Carl, Some problems of Erdős on the sum-of-divisors function. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B (2016), 1-26.
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {x | ∃ n, n - n.totient = x}ᶜ.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
It follows from a slight strengthening of the Goldbach conjecture that every odd number can be
written as $n - \phi(n)$.
In particular, we assume that every even number greater than 6 can be written as the sum of two
*distinct* primes, in contrast to the usual Goldbach conjecture that every even number greater than
2 can be written as the sum of two primes.

declarations.docstring:
**Erdős Problem 42**: Let M ≥ 1 and N be sufficiently large in terms of M. Is it true that for every
maximal Sidon set `A ⊆ {1,…,N}` there is another Sidon set `B ⊆ {1,…,N}` of size M such that
`(A - A) ∩ (B - B) = {0}`?

This was proved for all $M$ by GPT 5.5 Pro (prompted by Sandhu), see discussion thread for more details.
references: [erdosproblems.com/42](https://www.erdosproblems.com/42)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ M ≥ 1,
    ∀ᶠ (N : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
      ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.IsMaximalSidonSetIn N → ∃ B ⊆ Set.Icc 1 N, IsSidon B ∧ B.ncard = M ∧ (A - A) ∩ (B - B) = {0}

declarations.docstring:
A variant asking for explicit bounds on how large N needs to be in terms of M.

This version provides a constructive function f such that for all M ≥ 1 and N ≥ f(M),
every maximal Sidon set A ⊆ {1,…,N} has another Sidon set B ⊆ {1,…,N} of size M with
disjoint difference sets (apart from 0).
references: [erdosproblems.com/42](https://www.erdosproblems.com/42)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ f,
    ∀ (M N : ℕ),
      1 ≤ M →
        f M ≤ N →
          ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.IsMaximalSidonSetIn N → ∃ B ⊆ Set.Icc 1 N, IsSidon B ∧ B.ncard = M ∧ (A - A) ∩ (B - B) = {0}
