[Ga24] Gardam, G. (2024). Non-trivial units of complex group rings.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ G x,
  ∃ (_ : IsMulTorsionFree G),
    ∀ (p : ℕ), p = 0 ∨ Nat.Prime p → ∃ K x_3, ∃ (_ : CharP K p), ∃ u, ¬Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit ↑u

declarations.docstring: There is a counterexample to **Unit Conjecture** in any characteristic.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (p : ℕ),
  p = 0 ∨ Nat.Prime p → ∃ G x, ∃ (_ : IsMulTorsionFree G), ∃ K x_2, ∃ (_ : CharP K p), ∃ u, ¬Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit ↑u

declarations.docstring:
**The idempotent conjecture**

If `G` is torsion-free, then `K[G]` has no non-trivial idempotents.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : Field K] (G : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Group G],
  IsMulTorsionFree G → ∀ (a : MonoidAlgebra K G), IsIdempotentElem a → a = 0 ∨ a = 1

declarations.docstring: The Promislow group is torsion-free.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)
declarations.type_pretty: IsMulTorsionFree Kaplansky.PromislowGroup

declarations.docstring:
**The zero-divisor conjecture**

If `G` is torsion-free, then the group algebra `K[G]` has no non-trivial zero divisors.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplansky%27s_conjectures)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : Field K] (G : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Group G],
  IsMulTorsionFree G → NoZeroDivisors (MonoidAlgebra K G)

declarations.docstring: The **Köthe conjecture**: In any ring, the sum of two nil left ideals is nil.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] (I J : Ideal R), Koethe.IsNil I → Koethe.IsNil J → Koethe.IsNil (I + J)

declarations.docstring:
The **Köthe conjecture**: for any nil ideal `I` of `R`, the matrix ideal `M_n(I)` is a nil ideal
of the matrix ring `M_n(R)`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : TwoSidedIdeal R},
  Koethe.IsNil I → ∀ (n : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Fintype n], Koethe.IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.matrix n I)

declarations.docstring: The **Köthe conjecture**: every left nil radical is contained in the Köthe radical.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : Ideal R}, Koethe.IsNil I → ↑I ⊆ ↑(Koethe.KotheRadical R)

declarations.docstring: The **Köthe conjecture**: for any positive integer `n`, the Köthe radical of `R` is the matrix ideal `M_2(Nil*(R))`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : TwoSidedIdeal R},
  Koethe.IsNil I →
    ∀ (n : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Fintype n],
      TwoSidedIdeal.matrix n (Koethe.KotheRadical R) = Koethe.KotheRadical (Matrix n n R)

declarations.docstring:
The **Köthe conjecture**: for any nil ideal `I` of `R`, the matrix ideal `M_2(I)` is a nil ideal
of the matrix ring `M_2(R)`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : TwoSidedIdeal R}, Koethe.IsNil I → Koethe.IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.matrix (Fin 2) I)

declarations.docstring:
The **Amitsur Conjecture**: If `J` is a nil ideal in `R`, then `J[x]` is a nil ideal of the polynomial ring `R[x]`.
This is known to be false, see Agata Smoktunowicz, _Polynomial rings over nil rings need not be nil_.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6the_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] (J : TwoSidedIdeal R), Koethe.IsNil J → Koethe.IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.map Polynomial.C J)

declarations.docstring:
**The Komlós conjecture**

There exists a universal constant $K > 0$ such that for all $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and
all vectors $v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $\|v_i\|_2 \le 1$ (encoded here as
$\sum_j v_{ij}^2 \le 1$), there exist signs $\varepsilon_i \in \{-1, +1\}$ such that
$\left\|\sum_i \varepsilon_i v_i\right\|_\infty \le K$, i.e.
$\left|\sum_i \varepsilon_i v_{ij}\right| \le K$ for every coordinate $j$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrepancy_theory#Major_open_problems)

[W. Banaszczyk, *Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies*, Random Structures & Algorithms **12** (1998), 351–360](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1098-2418(199807)12:4%3C351::AID-RSA3%3E3.0.CO;2-S)
[J. Spencer, *Six standard deviations suffice*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **289** (1985), 679–706](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0784009-0)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ K,
  0 < K ∧
    ∀ (n m : ℕ) (v : Fin n → Fin m → ℝ),
      (∀ (i : Fin n), ∑ j, v i j ^ 2 ≤ 1) →
        ∃ ε, (∀ (i : Fin n), ε i = 1 ∨ ε i = -1) ∧ ∀ (j : Fin m), |∑ i, ε i * v i j| ≤ K

declarations.docstring:
**Banaszczyk's theorem**

There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for all $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and all vectors
$v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $\|v_i\|_2 \le 1$, there exist signs
$\varepsilon_i \in \{-1, +1\}$ such that
$\left\|\sum_i \varepsilon_i v_i\right\|_\infty \le C \sqrt{\log(n + 2)}$.
This is the best known bound towards the Komlós conjecture. (The shift $n + 2$ inside
the logarithm is a harmless normalization keeping it positive for $n \in \{0, 1\}$.)

[W. Banaszczyk, *Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies*,
Random Structures & Algorithms **12** (1998), 351–360.]
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrepancy_theory#Major_open_problems)

[W. Banaszczyk, *Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies*, Random Structures & Algorithms **12** (1998), 351–360](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1098-2418(199807)12:4%3C351::AID-RSA3%3E3.0.CO;2-S)
[J. Spencer, *Six standard deviations suffice*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **289** (1985), 679–706](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0784009-0)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ C,
  0 < C ∧
    ∀ (n m : ℕ) (v : Fin n → Fin m → ℝ),
      (∀ (i : Fin n), ∑ j, v i j ^ 2 ≤ 1) →
        ∃ ε, (∀ (i : Fin n), ε i = 1 ∨ ε i = -1) ∧ ∀ (j : Fin m), |∑ i, ε i * v i j| ≤ C * √(Real.log (↑n + 2))

declarations.docstring:
Sanity check: with no vectors at all ($n = 0$), the empty signed sum is $0$ in every
coordinate, so any constant bound holds.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrepancy_theory#Major_open_problems)

[W. Banaszczyk, *Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies*, Random Structures & Algorithms **12** (1998), 351–360](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1098-2418(199807)12:4%3C351::AID-RSA3%3E3.0.CO;2-S)
[J. Spencer, *Six standard deviations suffice*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **289** (1985), 679–706](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0784009-0)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (m : ℕ) (v : Fin 0 → Fin m → ℝ), ∃ ε, (∀ (i : Fin 0), ε i = 1 ∨ ε i = -1) ∧ ∀ (j : Fin m), |∑ i, ε i * v i j| ≤ 1

declarations.docstring:
For any tree $T$ with $n$ edges, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into
$2n+1$ edge-disjoint copies of $T$ via cyclic shifts of a single embedding.

The $2n+1$ copies are $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{2n}$ where $f_i(v) = f_0(v) + i$ for all vertices
$v$ — each copy is obtained by adding $i \pmod{2n+1}$ to every vertex of the base copy.
This is strictly stronger than `RingelConjecture.ringel_conjecture`.
references: A. Kotzig, cited in A. Rosa, *On certain valuations of the vertices of a graph*,
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type} [Finite V] (T : SimpleGraph V),
  T.IsTree →
    ∀ (n : ℕ),
      T.edgeSet.ncard = n →
        ∃ f,
          (∀ (i : Fin (2 * n + 1)) (v : V), (f i) v = (f 0) v + i) ∧
            (Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (SimpleGraph.map (f i) T).edgeSet (SimpleGraph.map (f j) T).edgeSet) ∧
              ⨆ i, SimpleGraph.map (f i) T = ⊤

declarations.docstring:
Let $G$ and $H$ be finite groups of the same order with
$\sum_{g \in G} \phi(|g|) = \sum_{h \in H} \phi(|h|)$,
where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function. Suppose that $G$ is simple. Is
$H$ necessarily simple?
references: [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v40)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (G H : Type) [inst : Group G] [inst_1 : Group H] [inst_2 : Fintype G] [inst_3 : Fintype H],
    Fintype.card G = Fintype.card H →
      ∑ g, (orderOf g).totient = ∑ h, (orderOf h).totient → IsSimpleGroup G → IsSimpleGroup H

declarations.docstring:
Let $G$ be a finite $p$-group and assume that all abelian normal subgroups of $G$
have order at most $p^k$. Is it true that every abelian subgroup of $G$ has order at most
$p^{2k}$?
references: [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v40)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (p : ℕ),
    Nat.Prime p →
      ∀ (G : Type) (x : Group G),
        IsPGroup p G →
          Finite G →
            ∀ (k : ℕ),
              (∀ (H : Subgroup G), H.Normal ∧ IsMulCommutative ↥H → Nat.card ↥H ≤ p ^ k) →
                ∀ (H : Subgroup G), IsMulCommutative ↥H → Nat.card ↥H ≤ p ^ (2 * k)

declarations.docstring:
Kummer–Vandiver conjecture states that for every prime $p$, the class number of the maximal
real subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ is not divisible by $p$.
-
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kummer%E2%80%93Vandiver_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (p : ℕ+), p.Prime → ¬↑p ∣ NumberField.classNumber ↥(NumberField.maximalRealSubfield (CyclotomicField ↑p ℚ))

declarations.docstring:
## Kurepa's conjecture

For all $n$, $$!n\not\equiv 0 \mod n$$

This appears as B44 "Sums of factorials."
in [Unsolved Problems in Number Theory](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0)
by *Richard K. Guy*
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → Kurepa.left_factorial n % n ≠ 0

declarations.docstring: Kurepa's conjecture for all integers greater than 2 is equivalent to the statement that $\gcd(n!, !n) = 2$ for all integers greater than 2.
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: (∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → Kurepa.left_factorial n % n ≠ 0) ↔ ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → n.factorial.gcd (Kurepa.left_factorial n) = 2

declarations.docstring: Kurepa's conjecture for all integers greater than 2 is equivalent to the conjecture restricted to primes greater than 2.
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: (∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → Kurepa.left_factorial n % n ≠ 0) ↔ ∀ (p : ℕ), 2 < p → Nat.Prime p → Kurepa.left_factorial p % p ≠ 0

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: for small values we can just compute that the conjecture is true
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → n < 50 → Kurepa.left_factorial n % n ≠ 0

declarations.docstring: An equivalent formulation in terms of the gcd of $n!$ and $!n$.
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → n.factorial.gcd (Kurepa.left_factorial n) = 2

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: for small values we can just compute that the conjecture is true.
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → n < 50 → n.factorial.gcd (Kurepa.left_factorial n) = 2

declarations.docstring: This statement can be reduced to the prime case only.
references: [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (p : ℕ), 2 < p → Nat.Prime p → Kurepa.left_factorial p % p ≠ 0

declarations.docstring:
Eisenstein's theorem (1852): an algebraic power series over $\mathbb{Q}[z]$ has bounded
denominators, i.e., there exists $N$ such that all coefficients lie in $\mathbb{Z}[1/N]$.
references: [Litt's problem 1](https://www.problemsilike.com/1)
Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam, Daniel Litt, "Algebraicity and integrality of solutions to differential equations", [arxiv/2501.13175](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13175)
Gotthold Eisenstein. "Über eine allgemeine Eigenschaft der Reihen-Entwicklungen aller algebraischen Funktionen", Bericht der Königl. Preuss. Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 1852
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (f : PowerSeries ℚ), IsAlgebraic (Polynomial ℚ) f → ∃ N, LamLitt.IsCoeffIntegralAdjointInvNat f N

declarations.docstring:
2) implies 1): if the coefficients of $f$ are in $\mathbb{Z}[1/N]$ for some $N$, then $f$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}[z]$.
Also the version of conjecture of Litt's problem 1 on his website.
references: [Litt's problem 1](https://www.problemsilike.com/1)
Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam, Daniel Litt, "Algebraicity and integrality of solutions to differential equations", [arxiv/2501.13175](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13175)
Gotthold Eisenstein. "Über eine allgemeine Eigenschaft der Reihen-Entwicklungen aller algebraischen Funktionen", Bericht der Königl. Preuss. Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 1852
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} (f : PowerSeries ℚ) (g : MvRatFunc (Fin (n + 1)) ℚ),
  LamLitt.IsSolutionOfAlgebraicODE n f g →
    ∀ (N : ℕ), LamLitt.IsCoeffIntegralAdjointInvNat f N → IsAlgebraic (Polynomial ℚ) f

declarations.docstring: Textbook implication: integrality (2) trivially implies ω(p)-integrality (3).
references: [Litt's problem 1](https://www.problemsilike.com/1)
Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam, Daniel Litt, "Algebraicity and integrality of solutions to differential equations", [arxiv/2501.13175](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13175)
Gotthold Eisenstein. "Über eine allgemeine Eigenschaft der Reihen-Entwicklungen aller algebraischen Funktionen", Bericht der Königl. Preuss. Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 1852
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : PowerSeries ℚ) (N : ℕ),
  LamLitt.IsCoeffIntegralAdjointInvNat f N →
    ∃ ω, LamLitt.omegaSuperlinear ω ∧ LamLitt.omegaIntegral ω fun x => (PowerSeries.coeff x) f

declarations.docstring:
3) implies 2): if the coefficients of $f$ satisfy the $\omega$-integrality condition for some superlinear $\omega$,
then there exists $N$ such that for all $n$, the $n$-th coefficient of $f$ is in $\mathbb{Z}[1/N]$.
references: [Litt's problem 1](https://www.problemsilike.com/1)
Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam, Daniel Litt, "Algebraicity and integrality of solutions to differential equations", [arxiv/2501.13175](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13175)
Gotthold Eisenstein. "Über eine allgemeine Eigenschaft der Reihen-Entwicklungen aller algebraischen Funktionen", Bericht der Königl. Preuss. Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 1852
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} (f : PowerSeries ℚ) (g : MvRatFunc (Fin (n + 1)) ℚ),
  LamLitt.IsSolutionOfAlgebraicODE n f g →
    ∀ (ω : Nat.Primes → ℤ),
      (LamLitt.omegaSuperlinear ω ∧ LamLitt.omegaIntegral ω fun x => (PowerSeries.coeff x) f) →
        ∃ N, LamLitt.IsCoeffIntegralAdjointInvNat f N

declarations.docstring:
The Lander–Parkin–Selfridge conjecture: if the sum of $n$ positive integer $k$-th powers
equals the sum of $m$ positive integer $k$-th powers, with all values on the left distinct from
all values on the right, then $n + m \geq k$.

Formally, for positive integers $k, n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences
$x : \{0, \ldots, n-1\} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $y : \{0, \ldots, m-1\} \to \mathbb{N}$
with $x_i > 0$, $y_j > 0$, and $x_i \neq y_j$ for all $i, j$, if
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} x_i^k = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} y_j^k,$$
then $k \leq n + m$.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (k n m : ℕ) (x : Fin n → ℕ) (y : Fin m → ℕ),
  (∀ (i : Fin n), 0 < x i) →
    (∀ (j : Fin m), 0 < y j) → (∀ (i : Fin n) (j : Fin m), x i ≠ y j) → ∑ i, x i ^ k = ∑ j, y j ^ k → k ≤ n + m

declarations.docstring:
Special case of the Lander–Parkin–Selfridge conjecture: there is no solution in positive
integers to
$$x_1^5 + x_2^5 + x_3^5 = y^5.$$
That is, for all $x_1, x_2, x_3, y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x_1, x_2, x_3, y > 0$,
$$x_1^5 + x_2^5 + x_3^5 \neq y^5.$$
This corresponds to the case $k = 5$, $n = 3$, $m = 1$ of the general conjecture,
where $n + m = 4 < 5 = k$ would be required to yield a counterexample.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (x₁ x₂ x₃ y : ℕ), 0 < x₁ → 0 < x₂ → 0 < x₃ → 0 < y → x₁ ^ 5 + x₂ ^ 5 + x₃ ^ 5 ≠ y ^ 5

declarations.docstring:
Conjecture 6.9 in [Wa2011]:
$$
\lim_{\substack{n \to \infty \\ n \text{ odd}}} \frac{1}{n} \log(z_n / n!) = -1
$$
It is not even known if this limit exists. Note that $z_n = 0$ for even $n$ (see `z_even`), so the
limit must be restricted to odd $n$; here we parametrise odd $n$ as $2k + 1$.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  Filter.Tendsto (fun k => 1 / (2 * ↑k + 1) * Real.log (↑(LatinSquare.z (2 * k + 1)) / ↑(2 * k + 1).factorial))
    Filter.atTop (nhds (-1))

declarations.docstring:
Conjecture 5.1 in [Wa2011]:
Every latin square has a near-transversal
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {n : ℕ}, True ↔ ∀ (L : LatinSquare n), ∃ ρ σ, IsNearTransversal L ρ σ

declarations.docstring: The smallest odd number for which this conjecture is not known is 11.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ (L : LatinSquare 11), ∃ σ, IsTransversal L σ

declarations.docstring:
Theorem 7.2 in [Wa2011]:
For all $n \geq 5$,
$$
15^{n/5} \leq T(n) \leq c^n \sqrt{n} \cdot n!
$$
where $c = \sqrt{\frac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{6}} \cdot e^{\sqrt{3}/6}$
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty:
have c := √((3 - √3) / 6) * Real.exp (√3 / 6);
∀ n ≥ 5, ↑(LatinSquare.T n) ∈ Set.Icc (15 ^ (↑n / 5)) (c ^ n * √↑n * ↑n.factorial)

declarations.docstring:
MOLS existence problem: determine exactly which orders `n` admit a complete set of `n - 1`
mutually orthogonal latin squares.

Equivalently, this asks for which orders affine planes of order `n` exist. Complete sets are known
for prime-power orders; the smallest currently unresolved order is `12`.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: sorry = {n | LatinSquare.HasCompleteMOLS n}

declarations.docstring:
The smallest unresolved case of the MOLS existence problem: whether there are `11` mutually
orthogonal latin squares of order `12`.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ LatinSquare.HasCompleteMOLS 12

declarations.docstring:
Conjecture 6.7 in [Wa2011]:
There exist real constants $0 < c_1 < c_2 < 1$ such that
$$
c_1^n n! \leq z_n \leq c_2^n n!
$$
for all odd $n \geq 3$.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ c₁ > 0,
    ∃ c₂ < 1,
      ∃ (_ : c₁ < c₂), ∀ n ≥ 3, Odd n → ↑(LatinSquare.z n) ∈ Set.Icc (c₁ ^ n * ↑n.factorial) (c₂ ^ n * ↑n.factorial)

declarations.docstring:
Conjecture 3.2 in [Wa2011]:
Each Latin square of odd order has at least one transversal.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {n : ℕ}, True ↔ Odd n → ∀ (L : LatinSquare n), ∃ σ, IsTransversal L σ

declarations.docstring: The conjecture is known to be true for $n \leq 9$.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ n ≤ 9, Odd n → ∀ (L : LatinSquare n), ∃ σ, IsTransversal L σ

declarations.docstring: The Cayley table of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for positive even $n$ has no transversals.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), LatinSquare.z (2 * (n + 1)) = 0

declarations.docstring:
The number of transversals of the Cayley table of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for odd $n$ forms
[OEIS A006717](https://oeis.org/A006717), starting with
$z(1) = 1, z(3) = 3, z(5) = 15, z(7) = 133$.
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: [LatinSquare.z 1, LatinSquare.z 3, LatinSquare.z 5, LatinSquare.z 7] = [1, 3, 15, 133]

declarations.docstring: The $0 \times 0$ Cayley table has exactly $1$ transversal (vacuously).
references: [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey." Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437. https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares
declarations.type_pretty: LatinSquare.z 0 = 1

declarations.docstring:
The Latin Tableau Conjecture: If G is the simple graph
of a Young diagram, then G is CDS-colorable.
references: [The Latin Tableau Conjecture](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v32i2p48)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (μ : YoungDiagram), μ.toSimpleGraph.CDSColorable

declarations.docstring:
**Lebesgue-Nagell Equation Conjecture**

For any odd prime $p$, the only integer solutions $(x, y)$ to the equation $x^2 - 2 = y^p$
are $(x, y) = (\pm 1, -1)$.

*Reference:* Ethan Katz and Kyle Pratt, "On the Lebesgue-Nagell equation $x^2 - 2 = y^p$",
[arXiv:2507.12397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12397)
references: [Wikipedia - Catalan's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_conjecture)
[arXiv:2507.12397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12397) (Lebesgue-Nagell equation)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (p : ℕ), Nat.Prime p → Odd p → ∀ (x y : ℤ), x ^ 2 - 2 = y ^ p ↔ (x = 1 ∨ x = -1) ∧ y = -1

declarations.docstring: The pair $(-1, -1)$ is a solution to $x^2 - 2 = y^p$ for any odd $p$.
references: [Wikipedia - Catalan's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_conjecture)
[arXiv:2507.12397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12397) (Lebesgue-Nagell equation)

declarations.docstring: The pair $(1, -1)$ is a solution to $x^2 - 2 = y^p$ for any odd $p$.
references: [Wikipedia - Catalan's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_conjecture)
[arXiv:2507.12397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12397) (Lebesgue-Nagell equation)

declarations.docstring:
If there exists a constant `c > 0` such that
`(n + 1).nth Nat.Prime - n.nth Nat.Prime < (n.nth Nat.Prime) ^ (1 / 2 - c)` for all large `n`,
then Legendre's conjecture is asymptotically true.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.
references: [Landau Problems Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Twin_prime_conjecture)
[Legendre Conjecture Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty:
(∃ c > 0,
    ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
      ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1)) - ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) < ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) ^ (1 / 2 - c)) →
  ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring: Does there always exist at least one prime between consecutive perfect squares?
references: [Landau Problems Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Twin_prime_conjecture)
[Legendre Conjecture Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring: Ferreira proved that the conjecture is true for sufficiently large n.
references: [Landau Problems Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Twin_prime_conjecture)
[Legendre Conjecture Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring:
Let `M(f)` denote the Mahler measure of `f`.
There exists a constant `μ>1` such that for any `f(x)∈ℤ[x], M(f)>1 → M(f)≥μ`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ μ,
  ∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
    μ > 1 ∧ (LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 → LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥ μ)

declarations.docstring: `μ=M(X^10 + X^9 - X^7 - X^6 - X^5 - X^4 - X^3 + X + 1)` is the best value for `lehmer_mahler_measure_problem`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
  LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 →
    LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥
      LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.lehmerPolynomial

declarations.docstring: If $f$ is not reciprocal and $M(f) > 1$ then $M(f) \ge M(X^3 - X - 1)$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
  LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 →
    f.reverse ≠ f →
      LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥
        LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ (Polynomial.X ^ 3 - Polynomial.X - 1)

declarations.docstring: If all the coefficients of $f$ are odd and $M(f) > 1$, then $M(f) \ge M(X^2 - X - 1)$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
  LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 →
    LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.Polynomial.HasOddCoeffs f →
      LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥
        LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ (Polynomial.X ^ 2 - Polynomial.X - 1)

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist a composite number $n > 1$ such that Euler’s totient function
$\varphi(n)$ divides $n - 1$?
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer%27s_totient_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ n > 1, ¬Prime n ∧ n.totient ∣ n - 1

declarations.docstring:
An abelian group is a Leinster group if and only if it is cyclic with order equal
to a perfect number.

Reference: Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". Theorem 2.1.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster_group)
Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". [arXiv:math/0104012](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104012)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (G : Type u_1) [inst : CommGroup G] [inst_1 : Fintype G],
  LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G ↔ IsCyclic G ∧ (Fintype.card G).Perfect

declarations.docstring:
Cyclic groups of perfect number order are Leinster groups.

This follows from the fact that for a cyclic group, all subgroups are normal and correspond
to divisors of the group order, and a number is perfect if and only if the sum of its divisors
(including itself) equals twice the number.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster_group)
Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". [arXiv:math/0104012](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104012)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (G : Type u_1) [inst : Group G] [inst_1 : Fintype G] [IsCyclic G],
  (Fintype.card G).Perfect → LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G

declarations.docstring:
The dihedral group `DihedralGroup n` (of order `2n`) is a Leinster group if and only if `n` is
an odd perfect number. This gives a one-to-one correspondence between dihedral Leinster groups
and odd perfect numbers.

In particular, the existence of odd perfect numbers is equivalent to the existence of
dihedral Leinster groups.

Reference: Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups".
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster_group)
Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". [arXiv:math/0104012](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104012)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ) [inst : NeZero n], LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster (DihedralGroup n) ↔ n.Perfect ∧ Odd n

declarations.docstring:
Non-abelian Leinster groups exist.

For example, `S₃ × C₅` (order 30) and `A₅ × C₁₅₁₂₈` are Leinster groups.

Reference: Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups".
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster_group)
Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". [arXiv:math/0104012](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104012)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ G x x_1, LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G ∧ ¬∀ (a b : G), a * b = b * a

declarations.docstring:
**Conjecture:** Are there infinitely many Leinster groups?

This asks whether there exist infinitely many (non-isomorphic) finite groups that are
Leinster groups.

Formalized via the negation of "Does there exist an n such that all Leinster groups have
order less than n".
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster_group)
Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". [arXiv:math/0104012](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0104012)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ¬∃ n, ∀ (G : Type) (x : Group G) (x_1 : Fintype G), LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G → Fintype.card G < n

declarations.docstring: For all odd integers $n ≥ 7$ there are prime numbers $p,q$ such that $n = p+2q$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Lemoine#Lemoine's_conjecture_and_extensions)
[Ki85] Kiltinen, J. and Young P. (1985). Goldbach, Lemoine, and a Know/Don't Know Problem.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 6 < n → Odd n → ∃ p q, Nat.Prime p ∧ Nat.Prime q ∧ p + 2 * q = n

declarations.docstring:
For all odd integers $n ≥ 9$ there are odd prime numbers $p,q,r,s$ and natural numbers $a,b$
such that $p+2q = n$, $2+pq = 2^a+r$, $2p+q = 2^b+s$
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Lemoine#Lemoine's_conjecture_and_extensions)
[Ki85] Kiltinen, J. and Young P. (1985). Goldbach, Lemoine, and a Know/Don't Know Problem.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  8 < n →
    Odd n →
      ∃ p q r s a b,
        Lemoine.OddPrime p ∧
          Lemoine.OddPrime q ∧
            Lemoine.OddPrime r ∧ Lemoine.OddPrime s ∧ p + 2 * q = n ∧ 2 + p * q = 2 ^ a + r ∧ 2 * p + q = 2 ^ b + s

declarations.docstring:
For any two real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$,
$$
  \liminf_{n\to\infty} n\||n\alpha\||\||n\beta\|| = 0
$$
where $\||x\|| := \min(|x - \lfloor x \rfloor|, |x - \lceil x \rceil|)$ is the distance
to the nearest integer.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood_conjecture)
[Bernard Mathan and Olivier Touli´e, *Problem`emes diophantiens simultan´es*][mathantoilie2004]
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (α β : ℝ), Filter.liminf (fun n => ↑n * distToNearestInt (↑n * α) * distToNearestInt (↑n * β)) Filter.atTop = 0

declarations.docstring:
For real number $\alpha$ and prime $p$,
$$
  \liminf_{n \to\infty} n |n|_{p}\||n\alpha\|| = 0
$$
where $\||x\|| := \min(|x - \lfloor x \rfloor|, |x - \lceil x \rceil|)$ is the distance
to the nearest integer, and $|x|_{p}$ is the $p$-adic norm.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood_conjecture)
[Bernard Mathan and Olivier Touli´e, *Problem`emes diophantiens simultan´es*][mathantoilie2004]
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (α : ℝ) (p : ℕ),
  Nat.Prime p → Filter.liminf (fun n => ↑n * ↑(padicNorm p ↑n) * distToNearestInt (↑n * α)) Filter.atTop = 0

declarations.docstring:
Consider $n$ runners on a circular track of unit length. At the initial time
$t = 0$, all runners are at the same position and start to run; the runners'
speeds are constant, all distinct, and may be negative. A runner is said to be
lonely at time $t$ if they are at a distance (measured along the circle) of at
least $\frac 1 n$ from every other runner. The lonely runner conjecture states that each
runner is lonely at some time, no matter the choice of speeds.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_runner_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ) (speed : Fin n ↪ ℝ) (lonely : Fin n → ℝ → Prop),
  (∀ (r : Fin n) (t : ℝ), lonely r t ↔ ∀ (r2 : Fin n), r2 ≠ r → dist ↑(t * speed r) ↑(t * speed r2) ≥ 1 / ↑n) →
    ∀ (r : Fin n), ∃ t ≥ 0, lonely r t

declarations.docstring:
**Theorem 1.3 (Tao, 2017; arXiv:1701.02048).**
There exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$,
the gap of loneliness satisfies
$\delta_n \ge \frac{1}{2n} + \frac{c \log n}{n^2 (\log \log n)^2}$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_runner_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c,
  0 < c ∧
    ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
      LonelyRunnerConjecture.deltaGap n ≥ 1 / (2 * ↑n) + c * Real.log ↑n / (↑n ^ 2 * Real.log (Real.log ↑n) ^ 2)

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: the Lychrel iteration at `56` reaches a palindrome.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ k, LychrelNumbers.IsPalindrome10 (LychrelNumbers.lychrelStep^[k] 56)

declarations.docstring: An equivalent formulation of `no_lychrel_numbers_base10`.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty:
(∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n → ∃ k, LychrelNumbers.IsPalindrome10 (LychrelNumbers.lychrelStep^[k] n)) ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n → ¬LychrelNumbers.IsLychrel10 n

declarations.docstring: The first widely studied open case: whether `196` is a base-10 Lychrel number.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ LychrelNumbers.IsLychrel10 196

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: `56 → 121` in one Lychrel step.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty: LychrelNumbers.lychrelStep^[1] 56 = 121

declarations.docstring:
**Lychrel conjecture (base 10):** conjecturally, there are no Lychrel numbers in base 10.

Equivalently, every positive integer eventually becomes a palindrome under the Lychrel iteration.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n → ¬LychrelNumbers.IsLychrel10 n

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: `121` is a base-10 palindrome.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty: LychrelNumbers.IsPalindrome10 121

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: digit reversal of `120` is `21`.
references: [Wikipedia: Lychrel number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number)
[MathWorld: Lychrel Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LychrelNumber.html)
[OEIS A023108](https://oeis.org/A023108)
[OEIS A023109](https://oeis.org/A023109)
declarations.type_pretty: LychrelNumbers.rev10 120 = 21

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist a $3 \times 3$ matrix such that every entry is a distinct square,
and all rows, columns, and diagonals add up to the same value?

0 is excluded, as a Magic Square of Squares with 0 and 8 distinct squares is know is knownn.
See [Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
references: [Magic Square of Squares - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_square_of_squares)
[multimagie.com](http://www.multimagie.com/English/SquaresOfSquaresSearch.htm)
[Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
[Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ m t,
    Function.Injective2 m ∧
      (∀ (i j : Fin 3), 0 < m i j ∧ IsSquare (m i j)) ∧
        (∀ (i : Fin 3), ∑ j, m i j = t) ∧
          (∀ (j : Fin 3), ∑ i, m i j = t) ∧ m 0 0 + m 1 1 + m 2 2 = t ∧ m 0 2 + m 1 1 + m 2 0 = t

declarations.docstring:
Does there exist a $3 \times 3$ semi-magic square whose entries are all distinct positive
integer cubes? A square is semi-magic if all rows and columns sum to the same total.

More precisely, we seek a $3 \times 3$ matrix with entries $a_{ij}$ such that each
$a_{ij} = n_{ij}^3$ for some positive integer $n_{ij}$, all nine cubes are distinct,
and all row sums and column sums are equal.

*Reference:*
[Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
references: [Magic Square of Squares - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_square_of_squares)
[multimagie.com](http://www.multimagie.com/English/SquaresOfSquaresSearch.htm)
[Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
[Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ m t,
    Function.Injective2 m ∧
      (∀ (i j : Fin 3), ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ m i j = n ^ 3) ∧ (∀ (i : Fin 3), ∑ j, m i j = t) ∧ ∀ (j : Fin 3), ∑ i, m i j = t

declarations.docstring: The **Mahler Conjecture** states that there are no non-zero Z-numbers.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (x : ℝ), x ≠ 0 → Mahler32.IsZNumber x → False

declarations.docstring: If Mahler's conjecture is true, i.e. there are no Z-numbers, then `Ω(3/2)` exceeds `1/2`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: (∀ (x : ℝ), x ≠ 0 → Mahler32.IsZNumber x → False) → 1 / 2 < Mahler32.Ω (3 / 2)

declarations.docstring: It is known that for all rational `p/q > 1` in lowest terms, we have `Ω(p/q) > 1/p`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (p q : ℕ), 1 < q → p.Coprime q → q < p → 1 / ↑p < Mahler32.Ω (↑p / ↑q)

declarations.docstring: The MLC conjecture, stating that the mandelbrot set is locally connected.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set#Local_connectivity)
[arxiv/math/9902155](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9902155)
[mathoverflow/37229](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/37229/)
declarations.type_pretty: LocallyConnectedSpace ↑Mandelbrot.mandelbrotSet

declarations.docstring:
A stronger version of the MLC conjecture, stating that all multibrots are locally connected.
Note that we don't need to require `2 ≤ n` because the conjecture holds in the trivial cases `n = 0`
and `n = 1` too.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set#Local_connectivity)
[arxiv/math/9902155](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9902155)
[mathoverflow/37229](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/37229/)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), LocallyConnectedSpace ↑(Mandelbrot.multibrotSet n)

declarations.docstring:
The density of hyperbolicity conjecture, stating that the set of all parameters `c` for which
`fun z ↦ z ^ 2 + c` has an attracting cycle is dense in the Mandelbrot set.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set#Local_connectivity)
[arxiv/math/9902155](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9902155)
[mathoverflow/37229](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/37229/)

parameters `c` for which `fun z ↦ z ^ n + c` has an attracting cycle is dense in `multibrotSet n`.

declarations.docstring:
Let `D` be the diagonal group of `SL_n(ℝ)` where n ≥ 3.
Then any relatively compact `D`-orbit in `SL_n(ℝ) / SL_n(ℤ)` is closed.
references: [arxiv/2504.17644v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17644v3)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ},
  3 ≤ n →
    ∀ (g : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin n) ℝ ⧸ Subgroup.map (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.map (Int.castRingHom ℝ)) ⊤),
      IsCompact (closure (MulAction.orbit (↥(Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.diagonalSubgroup (Fin n) ℝ)) g)) →
        IsClosed (MulAction.orbit (↥(Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.diagonalSubgroup (Fin n) ℝ)) g)

declarations.docstring:
**Huang–Shi, Theorem 1.2**

Let `F` be a finite field of characteristic `p ∈ {3, 5, 7, 11}`, and set
`K = F((t⁻¹))`, `A = F[t]`. Let

* `D` be the diagonal subgroup of `SL₄(K)`,
* `Γ = SL₄(A)` the lattice subgroup embedded into `SL₄(K)` via the natural inclusion `A →+* K`.

Then there exists `z : SL₄(K)/Γ` such that the `D`-orbit of `z` has compact
closure but is not closed.
references: [arxiv/2504.17644v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17644v3)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (F : Type u) [inst : Field F] [Fintype F],
  ringChar F ∈ {3, 5, 7, 11} →
    ∃ z,
      IsCompact
          (closure (MulAction.orbit (↥(Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.diagonalSubgroup (Fin 4) (LaurentSeries F))) z)) ∧
        ¬IsClosed (MulAction.orbit (↥(Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.diagonalSubgroup (Fin 4) (LaurentSeries F))) z)

declarations.docstring:
Now a famous isoperimetric relation asserts that
(IR) $I^p(F) \ge \frac{1}{p} \mu_p(F) \log_p \mu_p(F)$
This relation is true for every family $F$ and every $p$. It is especially famous and simple when
$p=1/2$ and $\mu_p(F)=1/2$. In this case, it says that given a set of half the vertices of the
discrete cube $2^X$, the number of edges between $F$ and its complement is at least $2^{n-1}$.

*Note on translation:* We use `Real.logb p m` to represent the logarithm base $p$ directly.
The factor of $p$ in the denominator (equivalent to $1/p$ in front) is consistent with the
definition of `IsOptimal` used in the counterexample proof.
references: [mathoverflow/10799](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/10799) asked by user [*Gil Kalai*](https://mathoverflow.net/users/1532/gil-kalai)

[Optimal Monotone Families for the Discrete Isoperimetric Inequality](https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/ai/optimal-monotone-families-for-the-discrete-isoperimetric-inequality/) by *Gil Kalai* (2026), a Polymath project with AI agents
[An Isoperimetric Inequality for the Hamming Cube and Integrality Gaps in Bounded-Degree Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0603218) by *Jeff Kahn* and *Gil Kalai* (2006)
[A Proof of the Kahn–Kalai Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17207) by *Jinyoung Park* and *Huy Tuan Pham* (2022)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ),
  0 < p →
    p < 1 →
      ∀ (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))),
        have m := Mathoverflow10799.μFamily p F;
        Mathoverflow10799.edgeBoundary n p F ≥ m * Real.logb p m / p

declarations.docstring:
Problem: For every monotone increasing family $F$, given an interval $[s,t]$ of real numbers so
that $t/s > 1000 \log n$ we have some $p$ in the interval $[s,t]$ so that $F$ is optimal with
respect to $\mu_p$.

This was a "missing lemma" in the work of Kahn and Kalai on threshold behavior of monotone
properties. The related [Kahn–Kalai conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0603218) was
[settled by Park and Pham](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17207).

**This conjecture is false** without the additional assumption $\mu_t(F) = 1/2$.
A counterexample was found by Shlomo Perles (April 7, 2026).
references: [mathoverflow/10799](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/10799) asked by user [*Gil Kalai*](https://mathoverflow.net/users/1532/gil-kalai)

[Optimal Monotone Families for the Discrete Isoperimetric Inequality](https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/ai/optimal-monotone-families-for-the-discrete-isoperimetric-inequality/) by *Gil Kalai* (2026), a Polymath project with AI agents
[An Isoperimetric Inequality for the Hamming Cube and Integrality Gaps in Bounded-Degree Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0603218) by *Jeff Kahn* and *Gil Kalai* (2006)
[A Proof of the Kahn–Kalai Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17207) by *Jinyoung Park* and *Huy Tuan Pham* (2022)
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ),
    2 ≤ n →
      ∀ (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))),
        Mathoverflow10799.IsMonotoneIncreasing F →
          ∀ (s t : ℝ),
            0 < s → s ≤ t → t < 1 → t / s > 1000 * Real.log ↑n → ∃ p, s ≤ p ∧ p ≤ t ∧ Mathoverflow10799.IsOptimal p F

declarations.docstring:

conjecture, but with the additional assumption that $t$ is the critical probability for $F$,
namely $\mu_t(F) = 1/2$.

declarations.type_pretty:
sorry ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ),
    2 ≤ n →

          ∀ (s t : ℝ),

              s ≤ t →

                  Mathoverflow10799.μFamily t F = 1 / 2 →
                    t / s > 1000 * Real.log ↑n → ∃ p, s ≤ p ∧ p ≤ t ∧ Mathoverflow10799.IsOptimal p F

proven in [mathoverflow/260589](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/260589) by user

references: [mathoverflow/235893](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/235893)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ f, Mathoverflow235893.IsConnectedMap ⇑f ∧ ¬Mathoverflow235893.IsConnectedMap ⇑f.symm

declarations.docstring: Does there exist a category that is pretriangulated but not triangulated?
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (C : Type u_1) [inst : CategoryTheory.Category.{u_2, u_1} C] [inst_1 : CategoryTheory.Preadditive C]
    [inst_2 : CategoryTheory.Limits.HasZeroObject C] [inst_3 : CategoryTheory.HasShift C ℤ]
    [inst_4 : ∀ (n : ℤ), (CategoryTheory.shiftFunctor C n).Additive] [inst_5 : CategoryTheory.Pretriangulated C],
    CategoryTheory.IsTriangulated C

declarations.docstring:
Let $P(x), Q(x) ∈ ℝ[x]$ be two monic polynomials with non-negative coefficients.
If $R(x) = P(x)Q(x)$ is a $0,1$ polynomial (coefficients only from $\{0,1\}$), then $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$
are also $0, 1$ polynomials.
references: [mathoverflow/339137](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/339137)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (P Q R : Polynomial ℝ),
  P.Monic →
    Q.Monic →
      (∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) →
        (∀ c ∈ Q.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) →
          R = P * Q → Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne R → Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne P ∧ Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne Q

declarations.docstring:
Green's Open Problem 28 is the probabilistic reformulation of Mathoverflow 339137.

Suppose that $X, Y$ are two finitely-supported independent random variables taking integer values,
and such that $X + Y$ is uniformly distributed on its range. Are $X$ and $Y$ themselves uniformly
distributed on their ranges?

Mathematically, this equivalence is established via Probability Generating Functions (PGFs),
shifting the support to $\mathbb{N}$, and appropriately scaling the coefficients.
references: [mathoverflow/339137](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/339137)
declarations.type_pretty:
(∀ (P Q R : Polynomial ℝ),
    P.Monic →
      Q.Monic →
        (∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) →
          (∀ c ∈ Q.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) →
            R = P * Q →
              Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne R → Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne P ∧ Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne Q) ↔
  (True ↔
    ∀ (X Y : PMF ℤ),
      X.support.Finite ∧ Y.support.Finite ∧ Green28.IsUniformOnSupport (Green28.indepSum X Y) →
        Green28.IsUniformOnSupport X ∧ Green28.IsUniformOnSupport Y)

declarations.docstring: The Lebesgue measure of the a rectangle `r` is `r.width * r.height`
references: [mathoverflow/34145](https://mathoverflow.net/q/34145)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (r : Mathoverflow34145.Rectangle), Mathoverflow34145.lbMeasure r.toSet = ENNReal.ofReal |r.width * r.height|

declarations.docstring: `lbMeasure` is invariant under `rigidMotion start θ`.
references: [mathoverflow/34145](https://mathoverflow.net/q/34145)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (start : ℝ × ℝ) (θ : Real.Angle) (s : Set (ℝ × ℝ)),
  Mathoverflow34145.lbMeasure (Mathoverflow34145.rigidMotion start θ '' s) = Mathoverflow34145.lbMeasure s

declarations.docstring: `lbMeasure` is scaled by `scale`.
references: [mathoverflow/34145](https://mathoverflow.net/q/34145)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (x y : ℝ) (s : Set (ℝ × ℝ)),
  Mathoverflow34145.lbMeasure (Mathoverflow34145.scale x y '' s) =
    ENNReal.ofReal |x * y| * Mathoverflow34145.lbMeasure s

declarations.docstring: The Lebesgue measure of the unit square is `1`.
references: [mathoverflow/34145](https://mathoverflow.net/q/34145)
declarations.type_pretty: Mathoverflow34145.lbMeasure Mathoverflow34145.unitSquare = 1

declarations.docstring: Can a unit square be covered by rectangles of width `1 / (n + 1)` and height `1 / (n + 2)`?
references: [mathoverflow/34145](https://mathoverflow.net/q/34145)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∃ c, ∀ p ∈ Mathoverflow34145.unitSquare, ∃ n, p ∈ (c.rect n).toSet

declarations.docstring:
It is known that packing the rectangles into a square of side length `133/132` is possible.

Reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0097316594901163
references: [mathoverflow/34145](https://mathoverflow.net/q/34145)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c,
  (∀ (n : ℕ), (c.rect n).toSet ⊆ { width := 133 / 132, height := 133 / 132, start := (0, 0), rotation := 0 }.toSet) ∧
    c.IsPacking

declarations.docstring:

Reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167506008706009

declarations.type_pretty:

declarations.docstring:
Let $f : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,  n \geq 2$ be a $C^1$ function. Is it true that
$$\sup_{x \in \mathbb R^n}f(x) = \sup_{x\in \mathbb R^n} f(x+\nabla f(x))$$?

Answer: No. A counterexample in $\mathbb R^2$ is recorded in the linked formal proof.
references: [mathoverflow/347178](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/347178)
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ n ≥ 2,
    ∀ (f : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) → ℝ),
      ContDiff ℝ 1 f →
        (BddAbove (Set.range f) ↔ BddAbove (Set.range fun x => f (x + gradient f x))) ∧
          ⨆ x, ↑(f x) = ⨆ x, ↑(f (x + gradient f x))

declarations.docstring:
Let $f : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,  n \geq 2$ be a $C^1$ function. Is the boundedness of
$\sup_{x \in \mathbb R^n}f(x)$ and $\sup_{x\in \mathbb R^n} f(x+\nabla f(x))$ equivalent?

Answer: No. The same counterexample is recorded in the linked formal proof.
references: [mathoverflow/347178](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/347178)
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ n ≥ 2,
    ∀ (f : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) → ℝ),
      ContDiff ℝ 1 f → (BddAbove (Set.range f) ↔ BddAbove (Set.range fun x => f (x + gradient f x)))

declarations.docstring:
Let $f : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,  n \geq 2$ be a $C^1$ function. Does the equality
$$\sup_{x \in \mathbb R^n}f(x) = \sup_{x\in \mathbb R^n} f(x+\nabla f(x))$$
hold when both suprema are finite?
references: [mathoverflow/347178](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/347178)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ n ≥ 2,
    ∀ (f : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) → ℝ),
      ContDiff ℝ 1 f →
        BddAbove (Set.range f) →
          BddAbove (Set.range fun x => f (x + gradient f x)) → ⨆ x, f x = ⨆ x, f (x + gradient f x)

declarations.docstring: There exists a semiring with a unique left maximal ideal but more than one right maximal ideals.
references: [mathoverflow/486451](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/486451)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ R x, (∃! I, I.IsMaximal) ∧ ∃ I J, I.IsMaximal ∧ J.IsMaximal ∧ I ≠ J

declarations.docstring:
There exists a semiring with a unique left maximal ideal and a unique right maximal ideal
which are not the same as sets.

This has been shown by Goran Žužić and Moritz Firsching using an experimental pipeline:
An example is the monoid algebra of the monoid of maps from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$
over $\mathbb{N}$.
references: [mathoverflow/486451](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/486451)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∃ R x,
    ∃ (hI : ∃! I, I.IsMaximal) (hJ : ∃! J, J.IsMaximal), ↑(Exists.choose hI) ≠ MulOpposite.op ⁻¹' ↑(Exists.choose hJ)

declarations.docstring:
There exists a proper ideal `I` in a (commutative) total ring `R` of fractions that is an
invertible module. If `I ⊊ R` is such an example, `I` must have infinite order in the Picard group,
and `R` must not be Noetherian (otherwise it must be semi-local and therefore have trivial Picard
group).
references: [mathoverflow/507128](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/507128/embeddability-order-on-picard-groups)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ R x, ∃ (_ : IsFractionRing R R), ∃ I, I ≠ ⊤ ∧ Module.Invertible R ↥I

declarations.docstring:
Given a complex polynomial $p$ of degree $d ≥ 2$ and a complex number $z$
there is a critical point $c$ of $p$, such that $|p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| ≤ |p'(z)|$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_problem)
[The fundamental theorem of algebra and complexity theory](https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1981-04-01/S0273-0979-1981-14858-8/)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.degree →
    ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
      ∃ c,
        Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
          ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤ ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

declarations.docstring:
The following weaker version of the mean value problem has been proven.
Given a complex polynomial $p$ of degree $d ≥ 2$ and a complex number $z$
there a critical point $c$ of $p$, such that $|p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| ≤ 4|p'(z)|$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_problem)
[The fundamental theorem of algebra and complexity theory](https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1981-04-01/S0273-0979-1981-14858-8/)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.degree →
    ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
      ∃ c,
        Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
          ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤ 4 * ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

declarations.docstring:
The following tighter bound depending on the degree $d$ of the polynomial $p$,
in the case of $p$ only having real roots has been shown by Tischler.
$|p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| \le (d-1)/d \cdot |p'(z)|$
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_problem)
[The fundamental theorem of algebra and complexity theory](https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1981-04-01/S0273-0979-1981-14858-8/)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.natDegree →
    (∀ (x : ℂ), p.IsRoot x → x.im = 0) →
      ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
        ∃ c,
          Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
            ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤
              (↑p.natDegree - 1) / ↑p.natDegree * ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

declarations.docstring:
The following tighter bound depending on the degree $d$ of the polynomial $p$,
in the case of $p$ all roots having the same norm has been shown by Tischler.
$|p(z) - p(c)|/|z-c| \le (d-1)/d \cdot |p'(z)|$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_problem)
[The fundamental theorem of algebra and complexity theory](https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1981-04-01/S0273-0979-1981-14858-8/)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.natDegree →
    (∀ (x y : ℂ), p.IsRoot x ∧ p.IsRoot y → ‖x‖ = ‖y‖) →
      ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
        ∃ c,
          Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
            ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤
              (↑p.natDegree - 1) / ↑p.natDegree * ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

declarations.docstring:
The first five Catalan-Mersenne numbers $c_0, \ldots, c_4$ are known to be prime.
Catalan conjectured that they are prime "up to a certain limit".
Are all Catalan-Mersenne numbers $c_n$ with $n \geq 5$ prime?

declarations.docstring:
For any odd natural number `p` if two of the following conditions hold,
then all three must hold:
1. $2^p-1$ is prime
2. $(2^p+1)/3$ is prime
3. Exists a number `k` such that $p = 2^k \\pm 1$ or $p = 4^k \\pm 3$
references: [Wikipedia: Mersenne conjectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_conjectures)
[Wikipedia: Catalan's Mersenne conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan%27s_Mersenne_conjecture)
[MathWorld: Catalan-Mersenne Number](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Catalan-MersenneNumber.html)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (p : ℕ), Odd p → Mersenne.NewMersenneConjectureStatement p

declarations.docstring:

[Mills' constant](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/MillsConstant.html) on Wolfram MathWorld.
[Mills' constant is irrational](https://doi.org/10.1112/mtk.70027) by *Kota Saito*, Mathematika **71** (2025), no. 3, e70027, [arXiv:2404.19461](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19461).

[OEIS A051021](https://oeis.org/A051021) (decimal expansion of Mills' constant)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A > 1, Mills.IsMills A

What is the minimal area (or greatest lower bound on the area)
of a *convex* shape that can cover every unit-length curve?
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moser%27s_worm_problem)

declarations.docstring:
The minimal area of a convex shape that can cover every unit-length curve is attained.
This follows from the Blaschke selection theorem.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moser%27s_worm_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ bound, IsLeast {v | ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, Convex ℝ X ∧ MeasureTheory.volume X = v} bound

declarations.docstring:
0.232239 is a lower bound on the area of a convex set that covers all worms.

*Reference:*
Khandhawit, Tirasan; Pagonakis, Dimitrios; Sriswasdi, Sira (2013),
"Lower Bound for Convex Hull Area and Universal Cover Problems",
International Journal of Computational Geometry & Applications,
23 (3): 197–212, arXiv:1101.5638, doi:10.1142/S0218195913500076, MR 3158583, S2CID 207132316.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moser%27s_worm_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: 0.232239 ∈ lowerBounds {v | ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, Convex ℝ X ∧ MeasureTheory.volume X = v}

declarations.docstring:
There is a convex set of area 0.270911861 that covers all worms.

*Reference:*
Wang, Wei (2006), "An improved upper bound for the worm problem",
Acta Mathematica Sinica, 49 (4): 835–846, MR 2264090.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moser%27s_worm_problem)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ X,
  MeasurableSet X ∧
    Convex ℝ X ∧
      MeasureTheory.volume X = 0.270911861 ∧
        ∀ w ∈ MoserWorm.Worms, ∃ e v, LinearEquiv.det e.toLinearEquiv = 1 ∧ w ⊆ (fun x => e x + v) '' X

declarations.docstring: Divergence is additive at points where both vector fields are differentiable.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} {v w : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)} {x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)},
  DifferentiableAt ℝ v x → DifferentiableAt ℝ w x → ∇⬝ (fun y => v y + w y) x = ∇⬝ v x + ∇⬝ w x

declarations.docstring: The divergence of a constant vector field is zero.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {n : ℕ} (c x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)), ∇⬝ (fun x => c) x = 0

declarations.docstring: The divergence of a vector field is $0$ at points where `fderiv` has its junk value.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} {v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)} {x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)},
  ¬DifferentiableAt ℝ v x → ∇⬝ v x = 0

declarations.docstring: Divergence commutes with scalar multiplication at differentiability points.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} (c : ℝ) {v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)} {x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)},
  DifferentiableAt ℝ v x → ∇⬝ (fun y => c • v y) x = c * ∇⬝ v x

declarations.docstring: The divergence of the zero vector field is zero.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {n : ℕ} (x : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)), ∇⬝ 0 x = 0

declarations.docstring:
The **Noether Problem**: let `L` be the field of rational functions in `n`
indeterminates over `K`. Is it true that `L/K` has the Noether property?

Solution: False.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)
declarations.type_pretty:
False ↔
  ∀ (K L ι G : Type) [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
    [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

declarations.docstring:
One can find a counterexample to the Noether Problem's claim by considering a
rational function field in 47 indeterminates.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ K L ι G x x_1 x_2 x_3,
  ∃ (x_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι), Fintype.card ι = 47 ∧ ¬NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

declarations.docstring: The Noether problem has a positive solution in the four indeterminate case.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {K L ι : Type} {G : Type} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
  [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Fintype.card ι = 4 → NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

declarations.docstring: The Noether problem has a positive solution in the three indeterminate case.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {K L ι : Type} {G : Type} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
  [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Fintype.card ι = 3 → NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

declarations.docstring: The Noether problem has a positive solution in the two indeterminate case.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {K L ι : Type} {G : Type} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
  [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Fintype.card ι = 2 → NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

declarations.docstring:
If the index set `ι` is empty, then `IsRationalExtension K L ι` means that
`K, L` are isomorphic as `K` algebras.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (K : Type u_1) (L : Type u_2) (ι : Type u_3) [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Algebra K L] [IsEmpty ι]
  [NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Nonempty (L ≃ₐ[K] K)

declarations.docstring:
A quadratic number field `K` is isomorphic to the explicit quadratic field
`QuadraticAlgebra ℚ d 0` for some squarefree `d : ℤ` not equal to 1.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : NumberField K] [Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension ℚ K],
  ∃ d, d ≠ 1 ∧ Squarefree d ∧ Nonempty (K ≃+* QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (↑d) 0)

declarations.docstring: An integer `D` is a fundamental discriminant iff it is the discriminant of some number field.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {D : ℤ},
  NumberField.IsFundamentalDiscr D ↔
    ∃ K x, ∃ (x_1 : NumberField K), Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension ℚ K ∧ NumberField.discr K = D

declarations.docstring:
An integer `D` is a fundamental discriminant iff it is the discriminant of the explicit
quadratic field `QuadraticAlgebra ℚ d 0` for some squarefree `d : ℤ` not equal to 1.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {D : ℤ},
  NumberField.IsFundamentalDiscr D ↔
    ∃ d, ∃ (x : Fact (d ≠ 1)) (x_1 : Fact (Squarefree d)), NumberField.discr (QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (↑d) 0) = D

declarations.docstring:
A number field `K` is quadratic iff it is isomorphic to the explicit quadratic field
`QuadraticAlgebra ℚ d 0` for some squarefree `d : ℤ` not equal to 1.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : NumberField K],
  Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension ℚ K ↔ ∃ d, d ≠ 1 ∧ Squarefree d ∧ Nonempty (K ≃+* QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (↑d) 0)

declarations.docstring:
"No negative terms among the first 2^20 terms. Is the sequence nonnegative?"

Equivalently, the rational Dirichlet square root `f` is nonnegative at every
positive index. Informally, the proof constructs a strictly positive
multiplicative square root prime-power by prime-power using formal power
series, and then identifies it with the recursively defined sequence `f`.

The proof was obtained by exploiting the multiplicativity of A046644 and
reducing the problem to its values on prime powers. The resulting convolution
recurrence for the prime-power coefficients was recognized as a
formal-power-series identity. A positive coefficient sequence was constructed
through a differential equation for the generating series, extended
multiplicatively to all positive integers, and finally identified with the
recursively defined Dirichlet square root by uniqueness.

declarations.docstring:
Conjecture: the dyadic valuation of A93179(n) - 1 does not exceed 2^n - a(n).

A93179(n) is minFac(fermatNumber n), the smallest prime factor of the n-th Fermat number.
The conjecture states that if $P_n$ is the smallest prime factor of the $n$-th Fermat number,
then $\nu_2(P_n - 1) \le 2^n - a(n)$.
Substituting the definition of $a(n)$, this is equivalent to $\nu_2(P_n - 1) \le \lfloor \log_2(P_n) \rfloor$.

This is Conjecture 3.4 in [SA22].

declarations.docstring:
**Conjecture (A6697)**: The generating function for the number of subwords of length $n$
in the infinite word generated by $a \mapsto aab, b \mapsto b$ is
$$\sum_{n \geq 0} a_n x^n = 1 + \frac{1}{1-x} + \frac{1}{(1-x)^2}\left(\frac{1}{1-x} -
  \sum_{k \geq 0} x^{2^{k+1} + k}\right).$$

Equivalently, a(n) equals the n-th coefficient of this generating function.

However, the reference quoted in the OEIS sequence

> J.-P. Allouche and J. Shallit, "On the subword complexity of the fixed point of a → aab, b → b,
> and generalizations," arXiv:1605.02361 [math.CO], 2016.

provides an explicit formula
$$ a_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \min(2^i,n-i+1). $$

If one takes this as a definition of a(n) instead,
it becomes straightforward to prove the conjecture.
See https://github.com/AxiomMath/gdm-formal-conjectures/blob/main/docs/OeisA6697.md
for a formal proof of the generating function using this definition.

Hence, a formalization of [arXiv:1605.02361](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.02361)
would complete a formal proof as below.
references: [A6697](https://oeis.org/A6697)
J.-P. Allouche and J. Shallit, "On the subword complexity of the fixed point of a → aab, b → b, and generalizations," arXiv:1605.02361 [math.CO], 2016.
N. J. A. Sloane and Simon Plouffe, *The Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences*, Academic Press, 1995.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  ↑(OeisA6697.a n) =
    (PowerSeries.coeff n)
      ((1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ +
        PowerSeries.X * (1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ ^ 2 *
          ((1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ - ∑' (k : ℕ), PowerSeries.X ^ (2 ^ (k + 1) + k)))

references: [A6697](https://oeis.org/A6697)
J.-P. Allouche and J. Shallit, "On the subword complexity of the fixed point of a → aab, b → b, and generalizations," arXiv:1605.02361 [math.CO], 2016.
N. J. A. Sloane and Simon Plouffe, *The Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences*, Academic Press, 1995.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), List.count false (OeisA6697.finiteWord n) = 2 ^ n

references: [A6697](https://oeis.org/A6697)

declarations.docstring: The Bloch inner product is determined by the $(0,0)$ entry of the relative unitary.

    OpenQuantumProblem13.IsUnbiased (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseU ζ hζ) (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseU η hη)

`z` and `w`.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (z w : ℂ), (z * star w).re = z.re * w.re + z.im * w.im

declarations.docstring: The $(0,0)$ entry of the relative unitary is the overlap of the first columns.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (U V : OpenQuantumProblem13.UMat 2),
  OpenQuantumProblem13.relativeUnitary U V 0 0 =
    star (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.u0 U) * OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.u0 V +
      star (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.u1 U) * OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.u1 V

declarations.docstring: The relative unitary of a basis with itself is the identity matrix.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (U : OpenQuantumProblem13.UMat 2), OpenQuantumProblem13.relativeUnitary U U = 1

declarations.docstring:
If $\overline{\zeta}\,\eta = i$, then the relative unitary between the corresponding phase
bases is the qubit mutually unbiased overlap matrix.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {ζ η : ℂ} (hζ : star ζ * ζ = 1) (hη : star η * η = 1),
  star ζ * η = Complex.I →
    OpenQuantumProblem13.relativeUnitary (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseU ζ hζ)
        (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseU η hη) =
      !![OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω, star OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω;
        star OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω, OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω]

declarations.docstring: Scaling a phase matrix by $\omega$ produces a unitary matrix whenever the phase has unit modulus.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {ζ : ℂ},
  star ζ * ζ = 1 →
    OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω • OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix ζ ∈ Matrix.unitaryGroup (Fin 2) ℂ

declarations.docstring:
The relative product of two scaled phase matrices is obtained by scaling the corresponding
relative product of phase matrices.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (ζ η : ℂ),
  star (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω • OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix ζ) *
      OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω • OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix η =
    (star OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω * OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.ω) •
      !![1 + star ζ * η, 1 - star ζ * η; 1 - star ζ * η, 1 + star ζ * η]

declarations.docstring: The relative product of two phase matrices has the expected $2 \times 2$ form.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (ζ η : ℂ),
  star (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix ζ) * OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix η =
    !![1 + star ζ * η, 1 - star ζ * η; 1 - star ζ * η, 1 + star ζ * η]

declarations.docstring: If $\zeta$ has unit modulus, then the phase matrix is orthogonal up to the scalar factor $2$.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {ζ : ℂ},
  star ζ * ζ = 1 → star (OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix ζ) * OpenQuantumProblem13.Qubit.phaseMatrix ζ = 2 • 1

declarations.docstring:
Taking the star of a scalar multiple on the left and multiplying by another scalar multiple
collects the scalar factor as $\overline{a} a$.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (a : ℂ) (A B : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℂ), star (a • A) * a • B = (star a * a) • (star A * B)

declarations.docstring:
**Oppermann's Conjecture**:
For every integer $x \ge 2$, the following hold:
- There exists a prime between $x(x-1)$ and $x^2$.
- There exists a prime between $x^2$ and $x(x+1)$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppermann%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (x : ℕ),
  2 ≤ x → (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring: Ferreira proved that Oppermann's conjecture is true for sufficiently large x.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppermann%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ᶠ (x : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
  (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring: For every integer $x \ge 2$ there exists a prime between $x(x-1)$ and $x^2$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppermann%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (x : ℕ), 2 ≤ x → ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring: For every integer $x \ge 2$ there exists a prime between $x^2$ and $x(x+1)$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppermann%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (x : ℕ), 2 ≤ x → ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring: Oppermann's conjecture implies Brocard's conjecture.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppermann%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  1 ≤ n →
    (∀ (x : ℕ),
        2 ≤ x →
          (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p) →
      4 ≤ (Finset.filter Nat.Prime (Finset.Ioo (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n ^ 2) (Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1) ^ 2))).card

declarations.docstring: Oppermann's conjecture implies Legendre's conjecture.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppermann%27s_conjecture)
[Luan Alberto Ferreira, *Real exponential sums over primes and prime gaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08725)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  1 ≤ n →
    (∀ (x : ℕ),
        2 ≤ x →
          (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p) →
      ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_pebbling)
[Pebbling on Graph Products and Other Binary Graph Constructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07808)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (A : PebblingNumberConjecture.PebbleDistribution V) {v w : V},
  2 ≤ A v →
    G.Adj v w →
      PebblingNumberConjecture.IsPebblingMove G A fun u => if u = w then A u + 1 else if u = v then A u - 2 else A u

references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_pebbling)
[Pebbling on Graph Products and Other Binary Graph Constructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07808)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (A : PebblingNumberConjecture.PebbleDistribution V),
  PebblingNumberConjecture.IsReachable G A A

declarations.docstring: The pebbling number of the complete graph on `n` vertices is `n`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_pebbling)
[Pebbling on Graph Products and Other Binary Graph Constructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07808)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] [inst_1 : Fintype V],
  PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber (SimpleGraph.completeGraph V) = Fintype.card V

declarations.docstring:
The pebbling number conjecture:
the pebbling number of a Cartesian product of connected graphs is at most equal to the product
of the pebbling numbers of the factors. See
[Asplund, Hurlbert, and Kenter](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07808).
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_pebbling)
[Pebbling on Graph Products and Other Binary Graph Constructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07808)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] {W : Type} [inst_1 : Fintype V] [inst_2 : Fintype W] [inst_3 : DecidableEq W]
  (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W),
  G.Connected →
    H.Connected →
      PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber (G □ H) ≤
        PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber G * PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber H
