declarations.docstring:
**Infinitely many even perfect numbers conjecture.**
Are there infinitely many even perfect numbers?

This is equivalent to asking whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes,
since by the Euclid–Euler theorem an even number is perfect if and only if it
has the form $2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ where $2^p - 1$ is a Mersenne prime.

*Reference:*
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
[Wikipedia, Odd perfect numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number#Odd_perfect_numbers)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | n.Perfect ∧ Even n}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
**Infinitely many perfect numbers conjecture.**
Are there infinitely many perfect numbers?

*Reference:*
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
[Wikipedia, Odd perfect numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number#Odd_perfect_numbers)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | n.Perfect}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
A known result: If an odd perfect number exists, it must be of the form
$p^α * m^2$ where $p$ is prime, $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, $\alpha \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$,
and $p \nmid m$.

*Reference:* Euler's theorem on odd perfect numbers.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
[Wikipedia, Odd perfect numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number#Odd_perfect_numbers)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), Odd n → n.Perfect → ∃ p m α, Nat.Prime p ∧ ↑p ≡ 1 [ZMOD 4] ∧ ↑α ≡ 1 [ZMOD 4] ∧ ¬p ∣ m ∧ n = p ^ α * m ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
A known result: If an odd perfect number exists, it must be greater than $10^{1500}$
and must have at least 101 prime factors (including multiplicities).

*Reference:* Pascal Ochem, Michaël Rao (2012).
"Odd perfect numbers are greater than 10^1500"
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
[Wikipedia, Odd perfect numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number#Odd_perfect_numbers)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), Odd n → n.Perfect → n > 10 ^ 1500 ∧ n.primeFactorsList.length ≥ 101

declarations.docstring:
**Odd Perfect Number Conjecture.**
The Odd Perfect Number Conjecture states that all perfect numbers are even.

*Reference:*
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number#Odd_perfect_numbers)
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number)
[Wikipedia, Odd perfect numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number#Odd_perfect_numbers)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), n.Perfect → Even n

declarations.docstring:
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture states that for every real piecewise-polynomial function
`f : ℝⁿ → ℝ`, there exists a finite set of polynomials `gᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ[x₁, ..., xₙ]` such that
`f = supᵢ infⱼ(gᵢⱼ)`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce%E2%80%93Birkhoff_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ),
  PierceBirkhoff.IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f →
    ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ (x : Fin n → ℝ), f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, (MvPolynomial.eval x) (g i j)

declarations.docstring:
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 1`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce%E2%80%93Birkhoff_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
  PierceBirkhoff.IsPiecewisePolynomial f →
    ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ (x : ℝ), f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, Polynomial.eval x (g i j)

declarations.docstring:
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 2`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce%E2%80%93Birkhoff_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) → ℝ),
  PierceBirkhoff.IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f →
    ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ (x : Fin 2 → ℝ), f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, (MvPolynomial.eval x) (g i j)

declarations.docstring: Are there infinitely many tuples of three consecutive primes $(p, q, r)$ such that $r - p = 6$?
references: [Prime Triplet Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_triplet#Conjecture_on_prime_triplets)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {p | Prime p ∧ (Prime (p + 2) ∨ Prime (p + 4)) ∧ Prime (p + 6)}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
For any `k ≥ 2`, let `a₁,...,aₖ` and `b₁,...,bₖ` be integers with `aᵢ > 0`. Suppose that for
every prime `p` there exists an integer `n` such that `p ∤ ∏ i, (aᵢ n + bᵢ)`. Then there exist
infinitely many `n` such that `aᵢ n + bᵢ` is prime for all `i`.
references: [FLC07] Friedlander, J. B. and Luca, F. and Stoiciu, M., On the irrationality of a
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {k : ℕ},
  2 ≤ k →
    ∀ (a : Fin k → ℕ+) (b : Fin k → ℕ),
      (∀ (p : ℕ), Nat.Prime p → ∃ n, ¬p ∣ ∏ i, (↑(a i) * n + b i)) →
        {n | ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (↑(a i) * n + b i)}.Infinite

declarations.docstring: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p - 1$ is a perfect square? In other words: Are there infinitely many primes of the form $n^2 + 1$?
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%27s_problems#Near-square_primes)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ {n | Prime (n ^ 2 + 1)}.Infinite

declarations.docstring: The discriminant of `ℚ[√d]` for `d ≥ 2` squarefree congruent to 1 mod 4 is `d`.

declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {d : ℤ} [inst : Fact (Squarefree d)] [inst_1 : Fact (d ≠ 1)],
  d ≡ 1 [ZMOD 4] → NumberField.discr (QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (↑d) 0) = d

declarations.docstring: The discriminant of `ℚ[√d]` for `d ≥ 2` squarefree not congruent to 1 mod 4 is `4 * d`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty:

  ¬d ≡ 1 [ZMOD 4] → NumberField.discr (QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (↑d) 0) = 4 * d

declarations.docstring:
For a graph $G$, we define $\Delta(G)$ to be the maximum degree, $\omega(G)$ to be the size of the
largest clique subgraph, and $\chi(G)$ to be the chromatic number. Reed's omega, delta, and chi
conjecture states that $$\chi(G) \leq \lceil \frac{1}{2}(\omega(G) + \Delta(G) + 1) \rceil.$$

For a finite graph $G$, we define $\Delta(G)$ to be the maximum degree, $\omega(G)$ to be the
size of the largest clique subgraph, and $\chi(G)$ to be the chromatic number. Reed's omega,
delta, and chi conjecture states that $$\chi(G) \leq \lceil \frac{1}{2}(\omega(G) + \Delta(G) + 1) \rceil.$$

declarations.docstring:
The **Riemann Hypothesis**: all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have real
part $\frac{1}{2}$. That is, if $\zeta(s) = 0$, $s \neq 1$, and $s$ is not a trivial zero
$-2(n+1)$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\operatorname{Re}(s) = \frac{1}{2}$.

This is the official Millennium Prize Problem as posed by the
[Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/riemann.pdf).

This uses the `RiemannHypothesis` type from Mathlib, which is defined as
`∀ (s : ℂ), riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2`.
references: [The Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/riemann.pdf)
[Wikipedia: Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis)
[Wikipedia: Generalized Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Riemann_hypothesis)
[Wikipedia: Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function)
J. Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, Springer (Grundlehren 322), 1999, Chapter VII, §5.
D. A. Marcus, *Number Fields*, Springer (GTM 81), 1977, Chapter VII.
declarations.type_pretty: RiemannHypothesis

declarations.docstring:
For any tree $T$ with $n$ edges, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into
$2n+1$ edge-disjoint copies of $T$.

A "copy" of $T$ is the image $T.\text{map}(f_i)$ of $T$ under a vertex embedding
$f_i : V \hookrightarrow \text{Fin}(2n+1)$; the copies are pairwise edge-disjoint
and together cover every edge of $K_{2n+1}$.
references: G. Ringel, *Problem 25*, in *Theory of Graphs and its Applications*
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type} [Finite V] (T : SimpleGraph V),
  T.IsTree →
    ∀ (n : ℕ),
      T.edgeSet.ncard = n →
        ∃ f,
          (Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (SimpleGraph.map (f i) T).edgeSet (SimpleGraph.map (f j) T).edgeSet) ∧
            ⨆ i, SimpleGraph.map (f i) T = ⊤

declarations.docstring:
Sanity check pinning `Q` to a concrete value: among the first `6` terms of `24 n + 1`, namely
`1, 25, 49, 73, 97, 121`, exactly four are perfect squares (`1, 25, 49, 121`), so
`Q 6 24 1 = 4`. This validates the definition of `Q` and matches the claim that `24 n + 1` is the
extremal progression.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin%27s_conjecture)
[Ru60] Rudin, W., *Trigonometric series with gaps*, J. Math. Mech. 9 (1960), 203–227.
González-Jiménez, E. and Xarles, X., *On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions*, LMS J. Comput. Math. 17 (2014), 58–76.
declarations.type_pretty: RudinsConjecture.Q 6 24 1 = 4

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: there are no squares among the first `0` terms of any progression.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin%27s_conjecture)
[Ru60] Rudin, W., *Trigonometric series with gaps*, J. Math. Mech. 9 (1960), 203–227.
González-Jiménez, E. and Xarles, X., *On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions*, LMS J. Comput. Math. 17 (2014), 58–76.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (q a : ℕ), RudinsConjecture.Q 0 q a = 0

declarations.docstring: Sanity check: the progression $24 n + 1$ is non-trivial.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin%27s_conjecture)
[Ru60] Rudin, W., *Trigonometric series with gaps*, J. Math. Mech. 9 (1960), 203–227.
González-Jiménez, E. and Xarles, X., *On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions*, LMS J. Comput. Math. 17 (2014), 58–76.
declarations.type_pretty: RudinsConjecture.IsNontrivial 24 1

declarations.docstring:
**Rudin's conjecture.** The maximal number of squares among the first $N$ terms of a non-trivial
arithmetic progression grows at most like $\sqrt{N}$:
$$Q(N) = O(\sqrt{N}).$$
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin%27s_conjecture)
[Ru60] Rudin, W., *Trigonometric series with gaps*, J. Math. Mech. 9 (1960), 203–227.
González-Jiménez, E. and Xarles, X., *On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions*, LMS J. Comput. Math. 17 (2014), 58–76.
declarations.type_pretty: (fun N => ↑(RudinsConjecture.Qmax N)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun N => √↑N

declarations.docstring:
A stronger form of Rudin's conjecture: for every $N \ge 6$, the arithmetic progression
$24 n + 1$ attains the maximum $Q(N)$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin%27s_conjecture)
[Ru60] Rudin, W., *Trigonometric series with gaps*, J. Math. Mech. 9 (1960), 203–227.
González-Jiménez, E. and Xarles, X., *On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions*, LMS J. Comput. Math. 17 (2014), 58–76.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (N : ℕ), 6 ≤ N → RudinsConjecture.Q N 24 1 = RudinsConjecture.Qmax N

declarations.docstring:
The strongest form of Rudin's conjecture also asserts *uniqueness*: for $N \ge 6$, any non-trivial
arithmetic progression attaining the maximum $Q(N)$ has common difference $24$. (Its initial term
is then forced by $\gcd(24, a) = 1$; the progression $24n + 1$ is the canonical representative.)
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin%27s_conjecture)
[Ru60] Rudin, W., *Trigonometric series with gaps*, J. Math. Mech. 9 (1960), 203–227.
González-Jiménez, E. and Xarles, X., *On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions*, LMS J. Comput. Math. 17 (2014), 58–76.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (N : ℕ),
  6 ≤ N → ∀ (q a : ℕ), RudinsConjecture.IsNontrivial q a → RudinsConjecture.Q N q a = RudinsConjecture.Qmax N → q = 24

declarations.docstring:
Given any set of $n$ complex numbers $\{z_1, ..., z_n\}$ that are linearly independent over
$\mathbb{Q}$, the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(z_1, ..., z_n, e^{z_1}, ..., e^{z_n})$
has transcendence degree at least $n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schanuel%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ) (z : Fin n → ℂ),

If a finite set of polynomials $f_i$ satisfies both Schinzel and Bunyakovsky conditions,
there exist infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that $f_i(n)$ are primes for all $i$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schinzel%27s_hypothesis_H)

declarations.docstring:
The Scholz conjecture, also known as the Scholz-Brauer conjecture, asserts that
for every positive integer $n$, the addition-chain length of $2^n - 1$ is at most
$n - 1 + \ell(n)$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholz_conjecture)
[MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ScholzConjecture.html)

[Tall22](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13812) Amadou Tall. "The Scholz conjecture on addition chain is true for infinitely many integers with $\ell(2n) = \ell(n)$." _arXiv:2210.13812_ (2022). Also available as [ePrint 2023/020](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/020).
[OEIS A003313](https://oeis.org/A003313)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n → ScholzConjecture.additionChainLength (2 ^ n - 1) ≤ n - 1 + ScholzConjecture.additionChainLength n

declarations.docstring:
**Schur's Theorem (1924):**
Let `f_n(x) = ∑_{j=0}^n x^j/j!` be the `n`-th truncated
exponential polynomial over `ℚ`. Then for `n ≥ 2`:

- If `n ≡ 0 (mod 4)`, the Galois group of `f_n` is isomorphic to the alternating group `A_n`
- If `n ≢ 0 (mod 4)`, the Galois group of `f_n` is isomorphic to the symmetric group `S_n`
references: (https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2814220)

declarations.docstring:
**PSW conjecture** (Selfridge's test)
Let $p$ be an odd number, with $p \equiv \pm 2 \pmod{5}$, $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$
and $F_{p+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, then $p$ is a prime number.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Selfridge#Selfridge's_conjecture_about_primality_testing)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (p : ℕ), Selfridge.IsSelfridge p → Nat.Prime p

declarations.docstring:
Selfridge's test variant:
Let $p$ be an odd number, with $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{5}$, $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$
and $F_{p-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, then $p$ is a prime number.

This test does not work.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Selfridge#Selfridge's_conjecture_about_primality_testing)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ n, Selfridge.IsPseudoSelfridge n ∧ ¬Nat.Prime n

declarations.docstring:
Selfridge's test variant:
Let $p$ be an odd number, with $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{5}$, $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$
and $F_{p-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, then $p$ is a prime number.

The number $6601$ is a conterexample to this test satisfying $6601 ≡ 1 \mod 5$
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Selfridge#Selfridge's_conjecture_about_primality_testing)
declarations.type_pretty: Selfridge.IsPseudoSelfridge 6601 ∧ ¬Nat.Prime 6601 ∧ 6601 ≡ 1 [MOD 5]

declarations.docstring:
Selfridge's test variant:
Let $p$ be an odd number, with $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{5}$, $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$
and $F_{p-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, then $p$ is a prime number.

The number $30889$ is a conterexample to this test satisfying $30889 ≡ - 1 \mod 5$
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Selfridge#Selfridge's_conjecture_about_primality_testing)
declarations.type_pretty: Selfridge.IsPseudoSelfridge 30889 ∧ ¬Nat.Prime 30889 ∧ 30889 ≡ 4 [MOD 5]

Selfridge conjectured that the number of prime factors of the `n`-th Fermat number does not grow
monotonically in $n$.

declarations.docstring:
Selfridge conjectured that the number of prime factors of the `n`-th Fermat number does not grow
monotonically in $n$.

A sufficient condition for this conjecture to hold is that there exists a Fermat prime larger than
65537.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Selfridge#Selfridge's_conjecture_about_primality_testing)

declarations.docstring:
**Sendov's conjecture** states that for a polynomial
$$f(z)=(z-r_{1})\cdots (z-r_{n}),\qquad (n\geq 2)$$
with all roots $r_1, ..., r_n$ inside the closed unit disk $|z| ≤ 1$, each of the $n$ roots is at a
distance no more than $1$ from at least one critical point.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendov%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 ≤ n → Sendov.Nat.SatisfiesSendovConjecture n

declarations.docstring:
**Sendov's conjecture** states that for a polynomial
$$f(z)=(z-r_{1})\cdots (z-r_{n}),\qquad (n\geq 2)$$
with all roots $r_1, ..., r_n$ inside the closed unit disk $|z| ≤ 1$, each of the $n$ roots is at a
distance no more than $1$ from at least one critical point.

It has been shown that Sendov's conjecture holds for polynomials of sufficiently large degree.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendov%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, Sendov.Nat.SatisfiesSendovConjecture n

with all roots $r_1, ..., r_n$ inside the closed unit disk $|z| ≤ 1$, each of the $n$ roots is at a
distance no more than $1$ from at least one critical point.

It has been shown that Sendov's conjecture holds when the degree of $n$ is at most $9$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendov%27s_conjecture)

declarations.docstring:
`edgeCount` of `K_{2,2}` (complete bipartite graph on `Fin 2 + Fin 2`) is `4`.

The four edges are `{inl 0, inr 0}`, `{inl 0, inr 1}`, `{inl 1, inr 0}`, `{inl 1, inr 1}`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty: (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin 2)).edgeFinset.card = 4

declarations.docstring:
If the domain of `H` has at most one vertex, `H` has no edges.

**Proof.** `SimpleGraph.Adj` is irreflexive, so any adjacency `H.Adj u v` forces
`u ≠ v`; on a subsingleton that's impossible, so no edges exist.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type u_3} [inst : Fintype V] [Subsingleton V] (H : SimpleGraph V) [inst_2 : DecidableRel H.Adj],
  H.edgeFinset.card = 0

declarations.docstring:
**The `Hom(K_{2,2}, G)` decomposition.** The number of homomorphisms from
`K_{2,2}` to `G` equals `∑_{(a, b) ∈ W × W} |N(a) ∩ N(b)|^2`, where `N(v)` is the
neighbourhood of `v` in `G`. Equivalently, summing over *ordered* pairs
`(b₀, b₁) ∈ W × W` and counting common neighbours squared.

**Math.** A homomorphism `K_{2,2} →g G` is an assignment `f : Fin 2 ⊕ Fin 2 → W`
with `G.Adj (f (inl i)) (f (inr j))` for all `i, j ∈ Fin 2`. Equivalently, choose
`(a₀, a₁) := (f (inl 0), f (inl 1))` arbitrarily in `W × W` and require
`(f (inr 0), f (inr 1))` to both lie in `N(a₀) ∩ N(a₁)`. The count is thus
`∑_{(a₀, a₁)} |N(a₀) ∩ N(a₁)|²`.

**Proof.** Construct an explicit bijection
`(K_{2,2} →g G) ≃ Σ (p : W × W), (N(p.1) ∩ N(p.2)) × (N(p.1) ∩ N(p.2))`
by sending a homomorphism `f` to `⟨(f (inl 0), f (inl 1)), ⟨f (inr 0), f (inr 1)⟩⟩`.
The total cardinality of the sigma-product is then
`∑_p (Fintype.card (N(p.1) ∩ N(p.2)))² = ∑_p |N(p.1) ∩ N(p.2)|²`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {W : Type u_3} [inst : Fintype W] [inst_1 : DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  ↑((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin 2)).homCount G) = ∑ p, ↑(G.neighborFinset p.1 ∩ G.neighborFinset p.2).card ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
**Homomorphism count of `K_2` into `G` equals `2 · #edgeFinset`.**

A homomorphism `K_2 →g G` is the same data as an ordered pair `(f 0, f 1)` of distinct
vertices with `G.Adj (f 0) (f 1)`. These are in bijection with the `Dart`s of `G`, and
`#Darts(G) = 2 · #E(G)` by `dart_card_eq_twice_card_edges`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {W : Type u_3} [inst : Fintype W] [inst_1 : DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homCount G = 2 * G.edgeFinset.card

declarations.docstring:
If the domain of `H` has at most one vertex, every function `V → W` is a homomorphism
`H →g G`. Equivalently, `homCount H G = |W|^|V|`.

**Proof.** The adjacency `H.Adj u v` is irreflexive; on a subsingleton it is uninhabited,
so the homomorphism condition `H.Adj u v → G.Adj (f u) (f v)` is vacuous. Hence the
`coe : (H →g G) → (V → W)` map is a bijection.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V : Type u_3} {W : Type u_4} [inst : Fintype V] [inst_1 : Fintype W] [Subsingleton V] [inst_3 : DecidableEq V]
  [inst_4 : DecidableEq W] (H : SimpleGraph V) (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_5 : DecidableRel H.Adj]
  [inst_6 : DecidableRel G.Adj], H.homCount G = Fintype.card W ^ Fintype.card V

declarations.docstring:
**Case `H = K_2` (single edge): Sidorenko's inequality holds trivially with equality.**

When `H` is `K_2` (the single-edge graph on 2 vertices), `e(H) = 1`, so the RHS of Sidorenko's
inequality is just `t(K_2, G)^1 = t(K_2, G) = t(H, G)`, which equals the LHS. Hence the
inequality holds as equality.

The proof records that `(completeGraph (Fin 2)).edgeFinset.card = 1` and then reduces the claim
to `t(K_2, G) ≤ t(K_2, G)`, which is `le_refl`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {W : Type} [inst : Fintype W] [inst_1 : DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G ^ (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).edgeFinset.card ≤
    (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G

declarations.docstring:
**Case `H = K_{2,2}` (four-cycle, also called `C_4`): Sidorenko's conjecture holds, by
Cauchy–Schwarz.**

The textbook statement at `H = K_{2,2}` is
`t(K_2, G)^{e(K_{2,2})} = t(K_2, G)^4 ≤ t(K_{2,2}, G)`.

**Proof sketch.** Write `d(a) := G.degree a`. Then
- `homCount(K_2, G) = ∑_a d(a) = 2·|E(G)|` (handshaking).
- `homCount(K_{2,2}, G) = ∑_{b₀, b₁} |N(b₀) ∩ N(b₁)|²` (product structure of bipartite
  homomorphism).
- `∑_{b₀, b₁} |N(b₀) ∩ N(b₁)| = ∑_a d(a)²` (swap sums).
- Cauchy–Schwarz #1: `(∑_{b₀, b₁} |N(b₀) ∩ N(b₁)|)² ≤ |W|² · ∑_{b₀, b₁} |N(b₀) ∩ N(b₁)|²`.
- Cauchy–Schwarz #2: `(∑_a d(a))² ≤ |W| · ∑_a d(a)²`.
- Chain: `(∑_a d(a))⁴ ≤ |W|⁴ · homCount(K_{2,2}, G)`.
- Divide by `|W|^8` to get `t(K_2, G)^4 ≤ t(K_{2,2}, G)`.

The proof uses `Finset.sum_mul_sq_le_sq_mul_sq` (discrete Cauchy–Schwarz) from
`Mathlib.Algebra.Order.BigOperators.Ring.Finset`.

**Status (2026-04-22):** main theorem closed sorry-free. See [Si93].
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {W : Type} [inst : Fintype W] [inst_1 : DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G ^ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin 2)).edgeFinset.card ≤
    (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin 2)).homDensity G

declarations.docstring:
Consequence of `homDensity_le_one`: both sides of the Sidorenko K_{2,2}
inequality are bounded above by 1. This is a trivial consequence, recorded
as a sanity check on the helper infrastructure in
`FormalConjecturesForMathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.HomDensity`.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {W : Type u_3} [inst : Fintype W] [Nonempty W] [inst_2 : DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph W)
  [inst_3 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G ≤ 1 ∧ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 2) (Fin 2)).homDensity G ≤ 1

declarations.docstring:
**Sidorenko's conjecture (1993).**

For every finite bipartite simple graph $H$ and every finite simple graph $G$:
$t(H, G) \ge t(K_2, G)^{e(H)}$, where $K_2$ denotes the single-edge graph on 2 vertices
(i.e. `completeGraph (Fin 2)`).
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ {V W : Type} [inst : Fintype V] [inst_1 : Fintype W] [inst_2 : DecidableEq V] [inst_3 : DecidableEq W] [Nonempty W]
    (H : SimpleGraph V) (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_5 : DecidableRel H.Adj] [inst_6 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
    H.IsBipartite → (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G ^ H.edgeFinset.card ≤ H.homDensity G

declarations.docstring:
**Case: `H` is a tree (Sidorenko 1993).**

If `H` is a finite tree then Sidorenko's inequality holds.

**Proof idea (Sidorenko 1993):** by induction on the tree, applying Jensen / convexity. The
number of homomorphisms from a tree `T` with `v` vertices and `v - 1` edges into `G` factors
nicely in the degree sequence of `G`, and AM–GM / convexity gives the required lower bound.

**Current status (2026-04-22, partial):**
- The subsingleton base case (`|V(T)| ≤ 1`) is dispatched via `sidorenko_tree_subsingleton`.
- The main inductive step (leaf extraction + AM–GM on the degree sequence) is deferred;
  it requires a walk-parametrised homomorphism count for trees and a discrete Jensen
  inequality. See [Si93].

The full proof is left as `sorry`; the subsingleton case is closed.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V W : Type} [inst : Fintype V] [inst_1 : Fintype W] [inst_2 : DecidableEq V] [inst_3 : DecidableEq W] [Nonempty W]
  (H : SimpleGraph V) (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_5 : DecidableRel H.Adj] [inst_6 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  H.IsTree → (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G ^ H.edgeFinset.card ≤ H.homDensity G

declarations.docstring:
**Base case of Sidorenko for trees.** When the tree `H` has at most one vertex,
both sides of Sidorenko's inequality evaluate to `1` (there are no edges, and every
function is a homomorphism). Thus the inequality `1 ≤ 1` holds trivially.

This covers the `|V(T)| = 1` base case of the induction on tree size.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {V W : Type} [inst : Fintype V] [inst_1 : Fintype W] [Subsingleton V] [inst_3 : DecidableEq V]
  [inst_4 : DecidableEq W] [Nonempty W] (H : SimpleGraph V) (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_6 : DecidableRel H.Adj]
  [inst_7 : DecidableRel G.Adj], (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 2)).homDensity G ^ H.edgeFinset.card ≤ H.homDensity G

declarations.docstring:
**`K_{2,2}` count via a re-indexed sum.** Swapping the order of summation, the
`Hom(K_{2,2}, G)` count equals `∑_{a ∈ W} (G.degree a)²` summed over... wait, more
precisely: the sum `∑_{(b₀, b₁)} |N(b₀) ∩ N(b₁)|` (without the square) equals
`∑_a (G.degree a)²`, by swapping `(∑_{b₀, b₁} ∑_a [a ~ b₀][a ~ b₁]) = ∑_a (∑_b [a ~ b])²`.

This version of the identity is what appears in the Cauchy-Schwarz step.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidorenko%27s_conjecture)
[Si93] Sidorenko, A. (1993). "A correlation inequality for bipartite graphs." *Graphs Combin.* 9, pp. 201--204.
[CoFo10] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. (2010). "Bounds for graph regularity and removal lemmas." *Geom. Funct. Anal.* 22, pp. 1191--1256.
[KLL18] Kim, J.H., Lee, C., Lee, J. (2018). "Two approaches to Sidorenko's conjecture." *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 370, pp. 8515--8552.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {W : Type u_3} [inst : Fintype W] [inst_1 : DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph W) [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  ∑ p, ↑(G.neighborFinset p.1 ∩ G.neighborFinset p.2).card = ∑ a, ↑(G.degree a) ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
**The extended Sierpiński problem.** Is 271129 the second-smallest Sierpiński number?

Even if 78557 is confirmed as the smallest Sierpiński number, there could exist a composite
Sierpiński number $k$ with $78557 < k < 271129$. We formalize "second-smallest" as: the
least Sierpiński number $k$ such that there exists exactly one Sierpiński number below it.
references: [Wikipedia, Sierpiński number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number)
[Si60] Sierpiński, W., Elementary Theory of Numbers. Państwowe Wydawnictwo Naukowe, Warsaw (1960).
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ IsLeast {k | k.IsSierpinskiNumber ∧ ∃ k', k'.IsSierpinskiNumber ∧ k' < k} 271129

declarations.docstring:
**The prime Sierpiński problem.** Is 271129 the smallest prime Sierpiński number?

In 1976, Nathan Mendelsohn determined that the second provable Sierpiński number is the prime
$k = 271129$.
references: [Wikipedia, Sierpiński number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number)
[Si60] Sierpiński, W., Elementary Theory of Numbers. Państwowe Wydawnictwo Naukowe, Warsaw (1960).
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ IsLeast {k | k.IsSierpinskiNumber ∧ Nat.Prime k} 271129

declarations.docstring:
Selfridge proved in 1962 that 78557 is a Sierpiński number by showing that all numbers of the
form $78557 \cdot 2^n + 1$ have a factor in the covering set $\{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73\}$.
references: [Wikipedia, Sierpiński number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number)
[Si60] Sierpiński, W., Elementary Theory of Numbers. Państwowe Wydawnictwo Naukowe, Warsaw (1960).
declarations.type_pretty: Nat.IsSierpinskiNumber 78557

declarations.docstring:
**The Sierpiński problem (Selfridge's conjecture).** Is 78557 the smallest Sierpiński number?

Selfridge conjectured that 78557 is the smallest Sierpiński number. He proved in 1962 that
78557 is indeed a Sierpiński number by showing that all numbers of the form $78557 \cdot 2^n + 1$
have a factor in the covering set $\{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73\}$.
references: [Wikipedia, Sierpiński number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number)
[Si60] Sierpiński, W., Elementary Theory of Numbers. Państwowe Wydawnictwo Naukowe, Warsaw (1960).
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ IsLeast {k | k.IsSierpinskiNumber} 78557

declarations.docstring:
`F n` is the smallest number of vertices of a triangle-free graph
with chromatic number `n` and `f = 3`.
declarations.type_pretty: ℕ → ℕ

declarations.docstring: The smallest number of vertices of a triangle-free graph with chromatic number 4 and f=3 is at most 19.
declarations.type_pretty: SimpleGraph.F 4 ≤ 19

declarations.docstring: The smallest number of vertices of a triangle-free graph with chromatic number 3 and f=3 is 7.
declarations.type_pretty: SimpleGraph.F 3 = 7

declarations.docstring:
**Lemma 3.** For every `n` there exists a bipartite graph with
`8 n` vertices, minimum degree `n + 1`, and `f = 3`.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n → ∃ G x, G.IsBipartite ∧ G.minDegree = n + 1 ∧ G.degreeSequenceMultiplicity = 3

∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (G : SimpleGraph α) [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
  G.Connected →
    G.CliqueFree 3 →
      ∀ (v : α),
        ∃ β x H x_1 i,
          H.CliqueFree 3 ∧
            H.degree (i v) = G.degree v + 1 ∧
              (∀ (w : α), w ≠ v → H.degree (i w) = G.degree w) ∧
                let J := SimpleGraph.induce (Set.range ⇑i).compl H;
                J.degreeSequenceMultiplicity = 3 ∧ J.minDegree ≥ 2 * Fintype.card α

declarations.docstring:
**Theorem 1.** If a triangle-free graph has `f = 2`,
then it is bipartite, has minimum degree `1`, and
its degree sequence is compact.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (G : SimpleGraph α),
  G.Connected →
    ∀ [inst_2 : DecidableRel G.Adj],
      G.CliqueFree 3 → G.degreeSequenceMultiplicity = 2 → G.IsBipartite ∧ G.minDegree = 1 ∧ G.HasCompactdegreeSequence

declarations.docstring:
**Theorem 2.** Every triangle-free graph is an induced subgraph of one
with `f = 3`.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {α : Type u_1} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (G : SimpleGraph α) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
  G.Connected → G.CliqueFree 3 → ∃ β x H x_1 i, H.CliqueFree 3 ∧ H.degreeSequenceMultiplicity = 3

declarations.docstring:
Singmaster's conjecture: the number of times any number $t > 1$ appears in
Pascal's triangle is bounded.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singmaster%27s_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ C, ∀ t > 1, (Singmaster.solutions t).Finite ∧ (Singmaster.solutions t).ncard ≤ C

declarations.docstring:
**Six standard deviations suffice** (Spencer, 1985)

For every $n$ and every family of $n$ subsets $S_1, \dots, S_n$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$,
there is a colouring $\chi : \{1, \dots, n\} \to \{-1, +1\}$ such that
$\left|\sum_{j \in S_i} \chi(j)\right| \le 6\sqrt{n}$ for every $i$.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrepancy_of_hypergraphs#General_hypergraphs)
[J. Spencer, *Six standard deviations suffice*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **289** (1985), 679–706](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0784009-0)
[N. Bansal, *Constructive algorithms for discrepancy minimization*, FOCS 2010, 3–10](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS.2010.7)
[S. Lovett and R. Meka, *Constructive discrepancy minimization by walking on the edges*, SIAM J. Comput. **44** (2015), 1573–1582](https://doi.org/10.1137/130929400)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (n : ℕ) (S : Fin n → Finset (Fin n)),
  ∃ χ, (∀ (j : Fin n), χ j = 1 ∨ χ j = -1) ∧ ∀ (i : Fin n), |∑ j ∈ S i, χ j| ≤ 6 * √↑n

declarations.docstring:
**The random colouring bound**

There is a constant $K > 0$ such that for every $n$ and every family of $n$ subsets
$S_1, \dots, S_n$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, there is a colouring
$\chi : \{1, \dots, n\} \to \{-1, +1\}$ with
$\left|\sum_{j \in S_i} \chi(j)\right| \le K \sqrt{n \log(n + 2)}$ for every $i$.
This follows from a Chernoff bound applied to a uniformly random colouring, and is
the benchmark that Spencer's theorem improves upon by removing the logarithmic
factor. (The shift $n + 2$ inside the logarithm is a harmless normalization keeping
it positive for $n \in \{0, 1\}$.)
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrepancy_of_hypergraphs#General_hypergraphs)
[J. Spencer, *Six standard deviations suffice*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **289** (1985), 679–706](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0784009-0)
[N. Bansal, *Constructive algorithms for discrepancy minimization*, FOCS 2010, 3–10](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS.2010.7)
[S. Lovett and R. Meka, *Constructive discrepancy minimization by walking on the edges*, SIAM J. Comput. **44** (2015), 1573–1582](https://doi.org/10.1137/130929400)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ K,
  0 < K ∧
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (S : Fin n → Finset (Fin n)),
      ∃ χ, (∀ (j : Fin n), χ j = 1 ∨ χ j = -1) ∧ ∀ (i : Fin n), |∑ j ∈ S i, χ j| ≤ K * √(↑n * Real.log (↑n + 2))

declarations.docstring:
Sanity check: with no points and no sets ($n = 0$), the empty colouring works and
the bound $6\sqrt{0} = 0$ holds vacuously.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrepancy_of_hypergraphs#General_hypergraphs)
[J. Spencer, *Six standard deviations suffice*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. **289** (1985), 679–706](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1985-0784009-0)
[N. Bansal, *Constructive algorithms for discrepancy minimization*, FOCS 2010, 3–10](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS.2010.7)
[S. Lovett and R. Meka, *Constructive discrepancy minimization by walking on the edges*, SIAM J. Comput. **44** (2015), 1573–1582](https://doi.org/10.1137/130929400)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (S : Fin 0 → Finset (Fin 0)), ∃ χ, (∀ (j : Fin 0), χ j = 1 ∨ χ j = -1) ∧ ∀ (i : Fin 0), |∑ j ∈ S i, χ j| ≤ 6 * √0

declarations.docstring:
**Wichmann's conjecture on optimal rulers.** Every optimal ruler with more than $13$
segments is a Wichmann ruler $W(r, s)$ (up to reflection, i.e. reversing the segment list).
Posed by Wichmann [Wi63]; the finitely many known exceptions all have at most $13$ segments
(lengths $1, 13, 17, 23, 58$), and no further exceptions are known up to length $213$.
references: [Wi63] Wichmann, B. "A note on restricted difference bases." Journal of the London Mathematical Society 38 (1963): 465-466.
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_ruler)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {g : List ℕ},
  SparseRuler.IsOptimal g →
    13 < g.length → ∃ r s, g = SparseRuler.wichmannGaps r s ∨ g = (SparseRuler.wichmannGaps r s).reverse

declarations.docstring:
Sanity check: the Fano plane is an $S(2, 3, 7)$-Steiner system.

The Fano plane consists of $7$ blocks of size $3$ over $7$ points,
where every pair of points is contained in exactly one block.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)
[Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems) by Kunal Marwaha
declarations.type_pretty: SteinerSystems.SteinerSystem 2 3 7

declarations.docstring:
**There are infinitely many Steiner systems with $t = 4$.**

Keevash (2014) proved that for any fixed $t$ and $k$, a Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$
exists for all sufficiently large $n$ satisfying the necessary divisibility conditions.
Since there are infinitely many such admissible $n$, this implies infinitely many
$S(4, k, n)$ systems exist (for any fixed $k > 4$). The proof is nonconstructive.

Explicit examples include $S(4, 5, 11)$ (the unique system, related to the Mathieu
group $M_{11}$) and $S(4, 7, 23)$ (related to the Mathieu group $M_{23}$).
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)
[Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems) by Kunal Marwaha
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ S, S.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
**There are infinitely many Steiner systems with $t = 5$.**

Keevash (2014) proved that for any fixed $t$ and $k$, a Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$
exists for all sufficiently large $n$ satisfying the necessary divisibility conditions.
This settles the long-standing open problem of whether infinitely many $S(5, k, n)$
systems exist. The proof is nonconstructive.

Only two explicit examples are known: $S(5, 6, 12)$ and $S(5, 8, 24)$, both Witt
designs related to the Mathieu groups $M_{12}$ and $M_{24}$ respectively.
No Steiner system with $t \geq 6$ has been explicitly constructed, though Keevash's
result guarantees their existence nonconstructively as well.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)
[Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems) by Kunal Marwaha
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ S, S.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
Construct an $S(t, k, n)$-Steiner system with $n > k > t > 5$, $t < 10$, and $n < 200$.

No example of a Steiner system with $t > 5$ is known, despite a 2014 existence theorem
by Keevash showing that such systems must exist for sufficiently large $n$.

*Reference:* [Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems)
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)
[Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems) by Kunal Marwaha

declarations.docstring:
**Existence of $S(5, 6, 12)$**: The small Witt design.

There exists a unique Steiner system $S(5, 6, 12)$, known as the small Witt design.
It was constructed by Witt (1938) and is closely related to the Mathieu group $M_{12}$.
This is one of only two known Steiner systems with $t = 5$.

declarations.docstring:
Simple test example,
A Boolean function whose block sensitivity is strictly greater than
its sensitivity. Source: [Nisan1989](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/73007.73038).

`nisanExample(x) = 1` iff the Hamming weight of `x` is either
`n/2` or `n/2 + 1`. We assume `n` is a multiple of 4.
The function is symmetric, so its value only depends on the Hamming weight
of the input.
references: [Induced Subgraphs of Hypercubes and a Proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00847) by Hao Huang (see Section 3, Concluding Remarks)
[Variations on the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0354) by Pooya Hatami, Raghav Kulkarni, and Denis Pankratov (see Question 3.1)
[On the Degree of Boolean Functions as Real Polynomials](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01263419) by Noam Nisan, and Mario Szegedy (see Section 4, Open Problems)
declarations.type_pretty: (n : ℕ) → (Fin n → Bool) → Bool

declarations.docstring:
Assuming `n` is a multiple of 4, the block sensitivity of `nisanExample`
is `3n/4`, achieved by any `x` with Hamming weight `n/2`.
An optimal block configuration uses all `n/2` 1-bits as singleton blocks
and forms `n/4` disjoint size-2 blocks from the 0-bits.
references: [Induced Subgraphs of Hypercubes and a Proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00847) by Hao Huang (see Section 3, Concluding Remarks)
[Variations on the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0354) by Pooya Hatami, Raghav Kulkarni, and Denis Pankratov (see Question 3.1)
[On the Degree of Boolean Functions as Real Polynomials](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01263419) by Noam Nisan, and Mario Szegedy (see Section 4, Open Problems)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 4 ∣ n → StrongSensitivityConjecture.blockSensitivity (StrongSensitivityConjecture.nisanExample n) = 3 * n / 4

declarations.docstring:
Assuming `n` is a multiple of 4, the sensitivity of `nisanExample`
is `n/2`, achieved by any `x` with Hamming weight `n/2`.
references: [Induced Subgraphs of Hypercubes and a Proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00847) by Hao Huang (see Section 3, Concluding Remarks)
[Variations on the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0354) by Pooya Hatami, Raghav Kulkarni, and Denis Pankratov (see Question 3.1)
[On the Degree of Boolean Functions as Real Polynomials](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01263419) by Noam Nisan, and Mario Szegedy (see Section 4, Open Problems)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (n : ℕ), 4 ∣ n → StrongSensitivityConjecture.sensitivity (StrongSensitivityConjecture.nisanExample n) = n / 2

declarations.docstring:
Strong Sensitivity Conjecture,
for every Boolean function `f : {0,1}^n → {0,1}`,
`bs(f) ≤ s(f)^2`.

We call this the *strong* sensitivity conjecture because the original sensitivity
conjecture only asked for a polynomial bound in terms of `s(f)`. Huang's
celebrated result (often called the sensitivity theorem) gives a quartic bound,
`bs(f) ≤ s(f)^4`, thereby settling the original conjecture.
references: [Induced Subgraphs of Hypercubes and a Proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00847) by Hao Huang (see Section 3, Concluding Remarks)
[Variations on the Sensitivity Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0354) by Pooya Hatami, Raghav Kulkarni, and Denis Pankratov (see Question 3.1)
[On the Degree of Boolean Functions as Real Polynomials](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01263419) by Noam Nisan, and Mario Szegedy (see Section 4, Open Problems)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → Bool) → Bool),
  StrongSensitivityConjecture.blockSensitivity f ≤ StrongSensitivityConjecture.sensitivity f ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
$A$ and $B$ are sets of words of length $n$ over alphabet with $q \geq 1$ letters.
No suffix of a word in $A$ coincides with a prefix of a word in $B$.
Then $|A| \cdot |B|$ is at most $\frac{q^{2n}}{en}$.

This problem is from *Maximal sets of strings with no prefix-suffix overlap* and was proved in
*An isoperimetric inequality for word overlap*.
references: [X post by Dmitry Rybin](https://x.com/DmitryRybin1/status/2027278135847428577)
[Maximal sets of strings with no prefix-suffix overlap] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/508648/maximal-sets-of-strings-with-no-prefix-suffix-overlap) by *Dmitry Rybin*, MathOverflow (2026)
[An isoperimetric inequality for word overlap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20143) by *Dmitrii Zakharov* (2026)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n q : ℕ} (A B : Finset (Fin n → Fin q)),
  0 < q →
    0 < n → SuffixPrefixAvoidance.IsSuffixPrefixAvoiding A B → ↑A.card * ↑B.card ≤ ↑q ^ (2 * n) / (Real.exp 1 * ↑n)

declarations.docstring:
$A$ and $B$ are sets of words of length $n$ over alphabet with $q \geq 1$ letters.
No suffix of a word in $A$ coincides with a prefix of a word in $B$.
Then $|A| \cdot |B|$ is at most $\frac{q^{2n}}{n}$.
references: [X post by Dmitry Rybin](https://x.com/DmitryRybin1/status/2027278135847428577)
[Maximal sets of strings with no prefix-suffix overlap] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/508648/maximal-sets-of-strings-with-no-prefix-suffix-overlap) by *Dmitry Rybin*, MathOverflow (2026)
[An isoperimetric inequality for word overlap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20143) by *Dmitrii Zakharov* (2026)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n q : ℕ} (A B : Finset (Fin n → Fin q)),
  0 < q → 0 < n → SuffixPrefixAvoidance.IsSuffixPrefixAvoiding A B → ↑A.card * ↑B.card ≤ ↑q ^ (2 * n) / ↑n

declarations.docstring:
For every finite union-closed family of sets, other than the family containing only the empty set,
there exists an element that belongs to at least half of the sets in the family.

declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq n] {A : Finset (Finset n)} [Nonempty n],
  A ≠ {∅} → UnionClosed.IsUnionClosed A → ∃ i, 1 / 2 * ↑A.card ≤ ↑{x ∈ A | i ∈ x}.card

declarations.docstring:
If the UC conjecture is tight for some family `A` then $|A| = 2^k$ for some $k$.

Reference: Conjecture 3 in https://www.nieuwarchief.nl/serie5/pdf/naw5-2023-24-4-225.pdf.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-closed_sets_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq n] {A : Finset (Finset n)} [Nonempty n],
  A ≠ {∅} ∧ A ≠ ∅ →
    UnionClosed.IsUnionClosed A → (∀ (i : n), ↑{x ∈ A | i ∈ x}.card = 1 / 2 * ↑A.card) → ∃ k, A.card = 2 ^ k

declarations.docstring:
Roberts and Simpson [Ro10] showed that the union-closed sets conjecture holds for set families of
size at most 46.
Their method, however, combined with the result of [Vu17], further shows that it holds for `#A ≤ 50`
as well.
[Ro10] Roberts, Ian; Simpson, Jamie (2010). "A note on the union-closed sets conjecture" (PDF). Australas. J. Combin. 47: 265–267.
[Vu17] Vuckovic, Bojan; Zivkovic, Miodrag (2017). "The 12-Element Case of Frankl's Conjecture" (PDF). IPSI BGD Transactions on Internet Research. 13 (1): 65.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-closed_sets_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq n] {A : Finset (Finset n)} [Nonempty n],
  A ≠ {∅} → UnionClosed.IsUnionClosed A → A.card ≤ 50 → ∃ i, 1 / 2 * ↑A.card ≤ ↑{x ∈ A | i ∈ x}.card

declarations.docstring:

any larger constant, then the conjecture fails.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-closed_sets_conjecture)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {n : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq n] [Fintype n] (c : ℝ),
  1 / 2 < c →
    ¬∀ (A : Finset (Finset n)), A ≠ {∅} → UnionClosed.IsUnionClosed A → ∃ i, c * ↑A.card ≤ ↑{x ∈ A | i ∈ x}.card

declarations.docstring:

∀ {n : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq n] {A : Finset (Finset n)},

declarations.docstring:
Classical Voronovskaja theorem (α = 1).

For functions $f$ that are $C^2$ on $[0,1]$, the limit:
$$
n\bigl( B_n f(x) - f(x) \bigr)
\;\longrightarrow\;
\frac{1}{2}\, x(1 - x)\, f''(x)
$$
references: [Voronovskaja-type Formula for the Bézier Variant of the Bernstein Operators](https://www.math.bas.bg/mathmod/Proceedings_CTF/CTF-2010/files_CTF-2010/Open_problems.pdf), by *Ulrich Abel*, in *Constructive Theory of Functions, Sozopol 2010*.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
  ∀ x ∈ unitInterval,
    ContDiffOn ℝ 2 f unitInterval →
      have f'' := iteratedDerivWithin 2 f unitInterval x;
      Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑n * (VoronovskajaTypeFormula.bezierBernstein n 1 f x - f x)) Filter.atTop
        (nhds (1 / 2 * x * (1 - x) * f''))

declarations.docstring:
Conjecture: Voronovskaja-type formula for Bézier-Bernstein operators
with shape parameter $\alpha > 0$, $\alpha \neq 1$.

The source asks for sufficiently smooth functions. This concrete version uses
`ContDiffOn ℝ 2 f I` as a readable baseline regularity assumption; since the
domain is the compact interval $[0,1]$, this also explains why no separate
boundedness assumption is included here. The variants below record the unknown
smoothness threshold more explicitly.
references: [Voronovskaja-type Formula for the Bézier Variant of the Bernstein Operators](https://www.math.bas.bg/mathmod/Proceedings_CTF/CTF-2010/files_CTF-2010/Open_problems.pdf), by *Ulrich Abel*, in *Constructive Theory of Functions, Sozopol 2010*.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (α : ℝ),
  0 < α →
    α ≠ 1 →
      ∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
        ∀ x ∈ unitInterval,
          ContDiffOn ℝ 2 f unitInterval →
            Filter.Tendsto (fun n => √↑n * (VoronovskajaTypeFormula.bezierBernstein n α f x - f x)) Filter.atTop
              (nhds sorry)

declarations.docstring:
Variant of the Bézier-Bernstein Voronovskaja problem with the required smoothness order itself
left as an answer. Replacing `(answer(sorry) : ℕ × ((ℝ → ℝ) → ℝ → ℝ))` by a concrete value lets one
state the conjecture for a chosen regularity threshold.
references: [Voronovskaja-type Formula for the Bézier Variant of the Bernstein Operators](https://www.math.bas.bg/mathmod/Proceedings_CTF/CTF-2010/files_CTF-2010/Open_problems.pdf), by *Ulrich Abel*, in *Constructive Theory of Functions, Sozopol 2010*.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (α : ℝ),
  0 < α →
    α ≠ 1 →
      have p := sorry;
      have m := p.1;
      have limitFormula := p.2;
      ∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
        ∀ x ∈ unitInterval,
          ContDiffOn ℝ (↑m) f unitInterval →
            Filter.Tendsto (fun n => √↑n * (VoronovskajaTypeFormula.bezierBernstein n α f x - f x)) Filter.atTop
              (nhds (limitFormula f x))

declarations.docstring:
Variant of the Bézier-Bernstein Voronovskaja problem which treats "sufficiently smooth" as an
eventual condition in the smoothness order $m$: for all sufficiently large finite $m$, every
$C^m$ function on $[0,1]$ should have the asserted asymptotic formula.
references: [Voronovskaja-type Formula for the Bézier Variant of the Bernstein Operators](https://www.math.bas.bg/mathmod/Proceedings_CTF/CTF-2010/files_CTF-2010/Open_problems.pdf), by *Ulrich Abel*, in *Constructive Theory of Functions, Sozopol 2010*.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (α : ℝ),
  0 < α →
    α ≠ 1 →
      have limitFormula := sorry;
      ∀ᶠ (m : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
        ∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
          ∀ x ∈ unitInterval,
            ContDiffOn ℝ (↑m) f unitInterval →
              Filter.Tendsto (fun n => √↑n * (VoronovskajaTypeFormula.bezierBernstein n α f x - f x)) Filter.atTop
                (nhds (limitFormula f x))

declarations.docstring:
Existence-only version of the eventual-smoothness variant. This separates the first part of the
source problem, proving that the scaled sequence has some limit, from the stronger task of finding
an explicit expression for that limit.
references: [Voronovskaja-type Formula for the Bézier Variant of the Bernstein Operators](https://www.math.bas.bg/mathmod/Proceedings_CTF/CTF-2010/files_CTF-2010/Open_problems.pdf), by *Ulrich Abel*, in *Constructive Theory of Functions, Sozopol 2010*.
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (α : ℝ),
  0 < α →
    α ≠ 1 →
      ∀ᶠ (m : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
        ∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
          ∀ x ∈ unitInterval,
            ContDiffOn ℝ (↑m) f unitInterval →
              ∃ L,
                Filter.Tendsto (fun n => √↑n * (VoronovskajaTypeFormula.bezierBernstein n α f x - f x)) Filter.atTop
                  (nhds L)

declarations.docstring:
A prime $p$ is a Wall–Sun–Sun prime if and only if $L_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$, where $L_p$ is the
$p$-th Lucas number. It is conjectured that there is at least one Wall–Sun–Sun prime.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ p, IsWallSunSunPrime p

declarations.docstring:
A prime $p$ is a Wall–Sun–Sun prime if and only if $L_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$, where $L_p$ is the
$p$-th Lucas number. It is conjectured that there are infinitely many Wall-Sun-Sun primes.
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty: {p | IsWallSunSunPrime p}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
A Lucas–Wieferich prime associated with $(a,b)$ is an odd prime $p$, not dividing $a^2 - 4b$, such
that $U_{p-\varepsilon}(a,b) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ where $U(a,b)$ is the Lucas sequence of the first
kind and $\varepsilon$ is the Legendre symbol $\left({\tfrac {a^2-4b}{p}}\right)$.
The discriminant of this number is the quantity $a^2 - 4b$. It is conjectured that there are
infinitely many Lucas–Wieferich primes of any given non-one fundamental discriminant.

TODO: Source this conjecture
references: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ {D : ℤ},
  NumberField.IsFundamentalDiscr D → D ≠ 1 → {p | ∃ a b, a ^ 2 - 4 * b = D ∧ IsLucasWieferichPrime a b p}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
**Problem 4.1.** Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite union of intervals and $\nu$
a weak tiling measure for $\Omega$. Must $\mathrm{supp}(\nu)$ have bounded density?
references: [Geometric implications of weak tiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23631)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (Ω : Set ℝ),
    WeakTiling.IsFiniteUnionOfIntervals Ω →
      ∀ (ν : MeasureTheory.Measure ℝ), WeakTiling.IsWeakTilingMeasure Ω ν → WeakTiling.HasBoundedDensity ν.support

declarations.docstring:
**Problem 4.2.** Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite union of three or more
intervals. If $\Omega$ weakly tiles its complement, must it also tile its complement
properly?
references: [Geometric implications of weak tiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23631)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ),
    3 ≤ n →
      ∀ (Ω : Set ℝ),
        WeakTiling.IsUnionOfNIntervals n Ω →
          ∀ (ν : MeasureTheory.Measure ℝ), WeakTiling.IsWeakTilingMeasure Ω ν → ∃ T, WeakTiling.IsProperTiling Ω T

declarations.docstring:
**Problem 4.3.** Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite union of intervals and $\nu$
a weak tiling measure for $\Omega$. Must $\nu$ be expressible as a convex combination of
proper tiling measures?
references: [Geometric implications of weak tiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23631)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ (Ω : Set ℝ),
    WeakTiling.IsFiniteUnionOfIntervals Ω →
      ∀ (ν : MeasureTheory.Measure ℝ),
        WeakTiling.IsWeakTilingMeasure Ω ν →
          ∃ T c,
            (∀ (i : ℕ), WeakTiling.IsProperTiling Ω (T i)) ∧
              ∑' (i : ℕ), c i = 1 ∧
                ν =
                  MeasureTheory.Measure.sum fun i =>
                    ↑(c i) • MeasureTheory.Measure.sum fun t => MeasureTheory.Measure.dirac ↑t
